title: Should estimate include breakdown of costs? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kendrahhendra", "author_name": "Kendrah", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kendrahhendra", "date": "2022-12-01", "text": "We received a scope of work estimate from our GC for an apartment we are renovating down the hall from us to use as an office / laundry room / guest room.  The estimate is broken down into 9 different sections of work - site protection, general construction, bathroom, kitchenette, flooring, electrical...  Each section includes a detailed list of tasks.  But, there is no breakdown of the costs at all, just one lump sum for the entire contract $128K. Is this typical?  How detailed should a price breakdown be?  We are going to need to cut back on costs because he left off a lot of costs and once I have him add them in, I know this is going over our budget.  But, I have no way of knowing where to cut back because there are no subcategories of costs. If it is not typical, how much detail do I ask for?  I want to be reasonable.  I'm not trying to nickle and dime and I don't want to piss him off.  But, I also don't want to be taken for a ride if these are poor practices for an estimate.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~848525206", "author_name": "Joseph Corlett, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~848525206", "date": "2022-12-01", "text": "\" I'm not trying to nickle and dime...\" Make sure you convey that clearly please, because from this contractor's perspective, that's exactly what potential customers who want detailed itemized proposals will do with the information. When potential customers ask me how much their sink costs me, I tell them to look on Amazon and they'll get a good idea. Yes, I pay less than they would, but I buy 100K worth of sinks a year. When they do that, they'll get the same price I do. No, I'm not giving them the sink for the same price I paid for it; don't ask. I'm running a business here. Materials, labor, overhead, and profit. However, the new homeowners soon discovered that key areas like the kitchen and bathrooms weren\u2019t very functional and the previous renovation from 2006 was looking tired and bland. Wanting to improve both the aesthetics and functionality, they decided to engage the services of professional interior designers to bring their vision to life.  The whole home was renovated as a result with the kitchen/casual dining and family living room as priorities. KITCHEN / CASUAL DINING AND LIVING The kitchen underwent a complete renovation with the grey tiled floor as the only original feature that remains. The brief was to significantly improve both the aesthetics and functionality with a more interesting palette of light and dark colours and finishes.  The casual dining and living areas are much more inviting and used daily by the family. BEFORE     AFTER         Art credit - Tjala Tjawani 2015 synthetic polymer on canvas by Anyupa Stevens from the Nyapari community in SA. MAIN BATHROOM The main bathroom renovation included a change of layout.   It\u2019s now a more functional and inviting space with a larger open shower, freestanding bath and useful storage behind mirrored shaving cabinets.  Timber laminate adds warmth and texture, and the terrazzo tiles, black accessories and brass tapware fit well with the art deco features of the home. BEFORE   NEW PLAN   AFTER       BOYS BEDROOM This bedroom was a joy to design.  Our work focused on a cosmetic renovation including carpet, window coverings, paint, wallpaper, lighting, custom cabinetry, and full furnishing and styling. title: Return Vent (aka Wind Tunnel) in Ceiling | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-107854039", "author_name": "HU-107854039", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-107854039", "date": "2022-12-01", "text": "I have a new home and the builders \"smartly\" decided to put in a return vent on the ceiling of the first floor (HVAC is on the second floor), directly below the HVAC unit.  Every time the AC or heat kicks on it sounds like a wind tunnel.  I had a tech out for another issue and asked him about the noise.  After a rant about how stupid return vents in the ceiling are, he suggested that I try covering the vent (I have two other return vents on the second floor).  I was a little surprised by this advice, as I had heard that you should NEVER cover a return vent (albeit, he did say to monitor the unit after covering the vent - to make sure that it's not overheating).  Anyway, I was wondering if anyone has tried this.  If not, I was wondering if insulating the return duct upstairs would help with the noise (or if there are any other ways to make this darn thing quieter)?  Thanks in advance. On a slightly different note - should I be worried about this?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b472ea7b0388a7f5_0280-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mike-home", "author_name": "mike_home", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mike-home", "date": "2022-12-01", "text": "If the ceiling return is the only one for the first floor then you can't block it. I suspect a majority of the noise is due to return is too small for the amount of air the furnace needs to operate. Adding insulation is likely not going to help. I think  you will need to make the return duct larger and move the return grille away from the furnace as much as possible. This may mean opening up the ceiling on the first floor. I would also have an HVAC tech investigate if the blower speed could be reduced and still have the furnace operate at the rated temperature rise. The picture you show appears to be the furnace condensate drain line. The condensate is freezing. The furnace condensate can be acidic and could eat away at the insulation over time. You can add a flex pipe extension to the end of the PVC pipe so that the water if further away form the foundation and drains onto the grass. You need to be careful to position the extension so no water collects in it. If it does it might freeze and cause a blockage.", "images": []}}

From the street, it looks like a single story home, so I want to maintain the vertical siding to give the house the look of more height. The existing siding looks like Eichler siding, but I know it is not. I like the aesthetic of the existing 2\" o.c. (on center) vertical pattern, and would like to find a fiber cement product for maintenance reason that can achieve a similar siding look. In meeting with NW contractors, they all seem to work with cedar or James Hardie fiber cement products only. The aesthetic options for Hardie are disappointingly limited (especially for vertically installation), with the tightest spacing at 7\" or 8\". The wider spacing isn't ideal as the proportions will make the house look more chunky with the 12\" spacing loc-seam metal roof. I'm not a fan of board and batten, and even the suggestion of spacing the battens tighter than 12\" or 16\" were not recommended for potential installation issues by the contractor. Does a fiber cement product with close to a 2\" vertical spacing exist? I am willing to go with 4\" vertical cedar siding and deal with the long term maintenance, but I want to know if I have really exhausted my options with fiber cement. title: How to reduce humidity in sealed concrete cellar | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-785016898", "author_name": "Tyson T", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-785016898", "date": "2022-12-01", "text": "Hi, We have a safe room in our basement that we've converted into a storage area and cellar.  The room is solid concrete- floors, walls, ceiling and has one door.  You access the safe room behind a trick bookshelf in our basement.  I've ran into a moisture problem this winter.  The temperature in the fall and winter months is a pretty consistent 50 degrees, but the humidity is fluctuating between 88-98%.  Consequently, there is a musty smell and we've had a bit of mildew on some storage containers in there.  In the 2 corners of the ceiling that are against the outside (as in they don't share a wall with the house), there was some visible condensation.  I'm trying to figure out the most efficient and economical route to address this issue. There is one vent in the room that has a pipe attached to it and the pipe sticks up outside the back of  the house.  The original owner had attached some ducting to a small dekstop fan and attached that to the vent hole.  I recently stuck a box fan in the room to circulate some air, and replaced the small desk fan with a small ventilation fan used for grow tents to suck air from the safe room to the outside via that vent.  It has a much higher cfm than the desk fan, but I have not noticed any significant change in the humidity levels doing this.  Both fans have been running continuous for a week.  The condensation on the ceiling corners are much improved though. I have a standard dehumidifier coming in the next week to try out and I'll drain that straight into the floor drain in the room.  Does anyone have any other suggestions on how to reduce the humidity levels in a room like this econimically?  The room is roughly 1500cu/ft (14x14x7.5)  I stained and sealed the concrete floors when we purchased the house, and I was curious about whether using a product like DryLok on the walls and ceiling would offer any help?  I've ready using DryLok can sometimes make a humidity issue worse and I certainly don't want that in an already compromised room.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "davidpilati", "author_name": "David Cary", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/davidpilati", "date": "2022-12-02", "text": "Arguably, the contractor did not meet a standard - like code - that you should be able to hold him or her to. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~63358994", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~63358994", "date": "2022-12-03", "text": "Advance is not a cabinet coating, and is well under the durability of a true professional cabinet finish. Advance is a trim paint. It is popular with the DIY painting crowd because it is friendlier to the brush and roll skills of beginners who do not own sprayers, or want to deal with respirators and other professional risk mitigation PPE.  It has a really long open time, so self levels extremely well. That helps produce a nice smooth finish, without someone having a lot of experience in applying paint. That long open time has a price, in that it can have a lot of dust and debris in the finish if you do not have a clean work area. It also has a 30 day plus cure time, to reach full hardness, so requires gentle use until that hardness is reached. Dark colors can take longer than 30 days for cures. Professional cabinet coatings are often dry within an hour, and cured in 6. Many shops also use infrared cure systems to speed up even that quick drying time. Professional cabinet coatings, especially catalyzed or hardener activated ones,  are harder, more chemical resistant, and provide greater long term durability than homeowner grade trim paints. That is why that is why the pros use them! CV, or conversion varnish is a multi part catalyzed system that is riskier to everyone involved that the newer waterborne 2K (2 part) European derived opaque polyurethane coatings like Milesi, Renner, Envirolak, Ilva, Centurion, etc etc. Those have some risks as well, but far less than the old solvent based products. There are no zero risks, and if a homeowner is interested in professional coatings, I always suggest them being applied by the professionals who have the safety equipment and ventilation to do so. If an advanced skills homeowner wants to use pro coatings, they need to also have all of the pro equipment to do so. With at least 40 hours of practice in that properly fit respirator.  They also need to look at the pictures of injection injuries from paint sprayers before ever firing up their sprayer. Safety doing any of this work is a very serious thing. All cabinet coatings are a system of coatings. Not just the final finish coat. It all starts with a clean dry surface that gets sanded. And sanded. And sanded. With the correct sanding schedule for the type of wood, and the type of finish. Both those variables come into that sanding schedule. But, the sanding is whst makes the biggest difference in the final appearance, over any type of finish chosen. The sanding shows through. You have to do the work underneath the coating, for a good result. You can\u2019t make up for poor prep work with an expensive coating over the top.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-12-07", "text": "@Alex [Zone 6a Lithuania.] You're probably on the right track, but more info is required from the OP to confirm. In all likelihood, the issue is soil related and involves a high TDS/EC (salt) level. Root function limitations from lack of oxygen or root disease is almost certainly a part of the issue The soil looks like compacted sand. Residual deposits in the collection saucer bears witness to water being allowed to sit in the collection saucer until it evaporates. If true, a steady increase in TDS/ salts is assured unless the grower is using R/O water or some form of deionized water. I addressed how to deal with a nutritional issue in a temporal fashion, but if the grower wants to put the best foot forward, he would do well to make sure the grow medium is structurally sound and he can water to beyond the point of total soil saturation (so at least 20% of the total volume of water applied at any given watering session exits the drain hole) without concern that root function or health are negatively affected by excess water retention and an inadequate volume of air for extended intervals. I agree this is not something a change in fertilizer can fix, and it's not a magnesium deficiency in the sense that magnesium can be identified as the single most limiting factor, nor do leaves present as being deficient in Mg - not even close. If there are multiple deficiencies (probable), improvement can come only by supplying the nutrient most lacking (see Liebig's Law). Not yet mentioned is the fact that Mg is one of the mobile nutrients, and as such any deficiency would be more conspicuous in older foliage as the plant robs older leaves of their Mg content to use as building blocks for new leaves coming on line. This is not the case. As noted, this is one of those times where the best thing the grower can do is address the basics. * Make sure the plant is in an appropriate soil * Make sure the planting can tolerate the soil being flushed w/o sacrificing root function or health * Make sure watering intervals are appropriate and the plant is watered on an 'as needed' basis as opposed to on a schedule * Make sure water quality is appropriate * Make sure the plant is fertilized regularly with an appropriate fertilizer * Make sure root temperatures are reliably below 90*F/ 32*C (if watering properly and using a pot with gas permeable walls, root temps should remain 10-15* F below ambient temps) Al", "images": []}}

title: Which of your plants didn't perform well this year? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "dirty-gardener", "author_name": "dirtygardener", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dirty-gardener", "date": "2022-12-04", "text": "Climate change brought we North Central FL gardeners an overly hot spring, extended summer, and a fall that doesn't seem to know what it wants to be. I had some plants that usually do very well without much care, but they didn't do well this year. Two of my mature brugmansias (angel trumpets) didn't even put up root shoots as they usually do. In fact, the shoots they did put up were spindly and never got much taller than a couple of feet tall, no matter how much I fertilized them. One of them was 7 years old, though. I got it as a small cutting when I first moved here. It was beautiful last year, so I don't know if it was the heat or what that affected it. Not even my potted brugs bloomed like they should have, and my main Charles Grimaldi put up one pitiful shoot, then died. Luckily, I have another one in a container. My taro did not come up at all until early fall, and didn't grow. I'm digging them up this winter and putting them into another bed. It may have been because I didn't rake out the magnolia leaves from their bed this year. I don't think they like the acidity. But then, the Xanthasoma, which usually take over the courtyard, didn't do well either. Only one grew to a decent size, and there were very few babies. None of my magenta four-o'clocks grew well or bloomed, and my giant white one only bloomed sparingly. They are usually some of my most faithful plants, and the white one is usually huge and spreads like mad, despite my attempts to pick off as many seeds as possible. My potato mint in containers did well, but not the ones in the ground. None of them have bloomed yet. My forsythia sage just barely came up, didn't put out any runners and didn't bloom. That's being taken up too and put into a container. In the same bed, my golden shrimp plant refused to even put out any leaves. My red shrimp plant didn't even come back up this year. I have a feeling my large bed is overrun by roots and nematodes. I'm going to try to terrace it this year, put in some compost and see what happens. The blackberry lilies and ironweed did very well in that bed, though. Everything in the courtyard did well except my Everglades tomatoes, which is strange. I still have one spindly one trying to grow. They are usually huge by now. All in all, a disappointing year. On the upside, many things are blooming like mad with this nice, cool, sunny weather. title: Speaking of sugar (not that we were)... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "roxanna-gw", "author_name": "roxanna", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roxanna-gw", "date": "2022-12-04", "text": "Found a five-pound bag of white sugar that is rock-hard.  How do I fix it???  Hammer?  Grater?  Keep it as is to knock out a burglar??  Help, please!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jehanne-hansen", "author_name": "claudia valentine", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jehanne-hansen", "date": "2022-12-05", "text": "I have used the trick of the piece of apple or bread in brown sugar but have never tried it on white sugar.  The two different sugars seem to differ in that the brown sugar has a moisture content that, when it is left exposed, will  evaporate and the brown sugar will harden.  However, white sugar has no moisture in it and will harden up with moisture. Sure that this is simple chemistry of some explanation.  Maybe someone here can shed some light.  Is moisture really what you want to put into your white sugar?  It must be in the chemistry of crystals that the difference is.  Brown sugar has a certain degree of molasses left in it or added back in after the refining, thus the moisture.  White sugar is hard dry crystals and it has been my experience that white sugar will actually harden with moisture. I never tried softening up white sugar with this technique and really never thought about trying it, but we learned the brown sugar trick early in life. With hardened sugar I will always use something to break it up. I am not so proud that I cant be proved wrong, but putting moisture into white sugar seems so antithetical to my longtime experience with it. Drop a spoon of water into the sugar canister and you will find a little hardened lump will form as it dries.  The crystals have dissolved and are hardened into a little shiny sugar rock. I always give it whack with something hard to break it up.  But, if it has hardened into a large solid mass that may provide limited results to use it in baking.  You can still dissolve it in liquid and use it like that, in some applications.  It WILL dissolve in moisture and water. I have a few hard lumps in my white sugar bucket right now.  Maybe I will experiment. However, you can make your own shaped sugar cubes by moistening your white sugar  with a few drops of water and putting it into small molds and let it dry. main_question: {"author_id": "four-gw", "author_name": "four (9B near 9A)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/four-gw", "date": "2022-12-05", "text": "Am I correct in thinking that, while plants are blooming vigorously, their production of leaves decelerates? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-12-11", "text": "Pecking Order of Plant Parts Plant parts and processes which require an allotment of the plant's food/ energy are called energy sinks, and the strength of these energy sinks is organized into a distinct and fairly predictable pecking order: During periods of growth, energy is first allocated to respiratory function, i.e. to maintenance of living tissues, then, to production of fine roots, followed by flower and seed/fruit production, then primary growth (extension of both roots and shoots as well as an increase in foliage mass), then secondary growth (thickening), and finally, the synthesis of defensive chemicals. You're correct in the idea that removing reproductive parts like blooms and developing fruit/ seeds frees up energy which can then be allocated to sinks of lesser strength - primary growth (extension of both roots and shoots as well as an increase in foliage mass), then secondary growth (thickening), and synthesis of defensive chemicals. The pecking order is generally true, but not carved into stone. E.g., in some plants, as the summer solstice passes and day length diminishes (actually, it's the increase in the dark period), demand for energy for secondary growth increases at the expense of primary growth. This allows temperate plants to store energy for a winter of short days and low light intensity, dormancy if applicable, and the spring flush of new growth. Al", "images": []}}

I am thinking that is more rural and maybe more traditional in that sense and that I will surely find some there. I found not one there either!  And, there were no hand made signs directing you to them and no Boy Scouts selling anywhere in some church parking lot. Normally on a weekend day in December you will see any number of cars going by with trees strapped to the roof.   I saw exactly two!  Thats all.....two!   If I had of been in the right position I would have signaled to them to share where they got it from.   Most likely it was Lowes or HOme Depot. I am shocked at what a difference a couple of years makes. The people that sold in tree lots must have to buy a large number of them at one time, and, I am thinking that maybe as the market has shifted away from real trees that the whole manner of marketing has changed and it may no longer be profitable.  There were always lots of trees left on the lots. I knew that there have been fewer and fewer tree lots, but I was not prepared for NO tree lots! Maybe some parts of the country have a different dynamic going on. I dont want a tree, but I have always, for many years been able to pick up the leavings and cuttings that I use to do something special with and they give them for free if you ask. main_question: {"author_id": "mwallbrecht", "author_name": "mwallbrecht", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mwallbrecht", "date": "2022-12-06", "text": "I need some advice. Maybe from someone who is knowledgeable about engineered hardwood installation. We had old glue down engineered maple wood removed from our home, and we replaced it with French oak engineered wood flooring. I spent months and months researching different flooring brands, I looked at dozens of samples, I talked with friends and searched online forums, talked with 4 or 5 different flooring stores, and I ultimately decided on using California Classics Mediterranean line of flooring, based on the quality and great reputation of their flooring. I chose my flooring supplier/installer (they did both) based on recommendations of friends. This particular small family owned company installed flooring for 4 of my friends, and all were very happy. One friend also had the Mediterranean line installed by this company. The Mediterranean line recently had a new version come out called the Mediterranean 9.5, just a wider version of their regular 8\u201d line. I love the wider plank floors, but wasn\u2019t going to choose the 9.5\u201d due to higher cost. When I had the flooring company price it out for me, it was only $400 more total for the 9.5\u201d over the 8\u201d, so I decided to go for it and that is what I had installed, approx 1800sqft. Fast forward to after installation. Walking on it for a few days I started to notice several hollow spots, spread out in patches all over my new floor. We had glue down engineered wood before so I\u2019m familiar with how it should sound and feel to walk on. But I was hearing so many hollow spots, and I could also hear a crunching or cracking sound when I would step on the hollow spot! I marked out all the hollow spots I could find with blue tape and showed my installer, and they almost didn\u2019t believe me. But I took video of all the crunching sounds I could hear so there was no disputing it. They told me in 20 years of installation they have never had this issue before (lucky me!) They we\u2019re adamant that their install was done right, and that in fact they had to go buy a new trowel just for this floor since it was extra wide. Since it is a new line of floor, they have never installed this particular flooring so they are putting the blame onto the manufacturer. (And, I\u2019m aware that it is the risk I took choosing a flooring that was so new, and I regret my choice now but what can I do at this point). My flooring guys are honest people and they genuinely want to help make it right, so what they did was drill holes all over my brand new floor to inject a special glue onto the air spaces. This has helped in many of the spots, but there are a few areas that still have air pockets and crunch when I walk on them. They said the next thing to do would be to get the manufacturer to come take a look, but that would mean they would have to cut a strip of my floor out at my sliding door and my front door where they intentionally didn\u2019t leave the required gap (which is their usual practice of install) but would fail installation inspection from the manufacturer. I don\u2019t really want those spots cut out, because even if the manufacturer were to come what would they do? I am guessing they won\u2019t take responsibility and will try to put blame on the installation. And installers are adamant they did it correct. main_question: {"author_id": "ben-lunsford85", "author_name": "Ben Lunsford", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ben-lunsford85", "date": "2022-12-06", "text": "Is a building (commercial or residential) legally required to have an electrical supply? main_question: {"author_id": "klem1", "author_name": "klem1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/klem1", "date": "2022-12-06", "text": "I've been very pleased with h\u00fcgelkultur and been thinking of incorporating biochar with it and/or adding biochar to compost when stored.  Judging by cost if bought the stuff is like gold.   Lots of conflicting info coming from experts.  Some say it has no nutrients others call it fertilize.  Some say it accelerates deterioration others claim it causes wood to deteriorate extremely slow.   The way I figured to use it is dig a hole and fill with varying size wood,set wood on fire then cover it with dirt after it is burning well.  It's sorta sketchy as to whether it's necessary to extinguish fire with water to prevent total consumption.  I know from experience wood fence post can be preserved by charring before burying so I'm concerned wood will not rot if charred.  Anyone made and/or used biochar and if so what do you think?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "armoured", "author_name": "armoured", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/armoured", "date": "2022-12-07", "text": "@klem1, what specific advantages of biochar are you hoping to get over other soil amendments? What problems are you trying to solve? I think the short-cut answer is mostly that msot of the perceived benefits of biochar can be achieved with hugel or other organic amendments - particularly moderating soil ph, improved nutrient profiles, etc. Personally the only large-scale credible claims I've heard to my ear are longevity (if properly done, in a C-form that not many organisms eat). And here we're talking in some circumstances (not much air), and timeframes well beyond your lifetime. title: Cooking with Cannabis | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "fawnridge69", "author_name": "fawnridge (Ricky)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fawnridge69", "date": "2022-12-06", "text": "A while back, I posted a thread about baking edibles. Since cooking with cannabis has become a thing, I thought I'd share some of my experiences with the magical herb. First and foremost, it's important to keep in mind that whatever you cook with cannabis is going to taste like the plant. Cannabis is not a delicate herb and the flavors are easily overpowering. Of course, the aftereffects are also quite striking, but that's not really the goal of cooking with weed. (Although it's an honorable one.) If you're a regular cannabis smoker or edible consumer, I would not recommend wasting your valuable product on soups and sauces. The amount of THC you'll ingest will probably be far less than your usual dosage and you'll be less than pleased with the results. On the other hand, if you're a casual, infrequent user, you'll definitely get a buzz. I had hoped that as more states granted legalizing that the prices would come down. Sadly, greed is still a factor and if you're cooking on a budget, spending the extra cash for some herb is not the best use of your money. Use ONLY flower. Lots of cooks on television and the internet are all about the terpines and the flavor you get from the leaves. To my ancient tastebuds, that flavor is no different than chewing on lawn clippings. And grind the flower to a fine powder to get the maximum return on both flavor and THC. Cannabis fails as a dry rub and even as a standalone ingredient. It's best used in a sauce where low heat, time, and fat will bring out the power and the essence. Butter, oil, or any kind of animal fat in a skillet with ground cannabis is the beginning. To it, add whatever you like. Strain the mixture through fine cheese cloth when the sauce is done. It also works quite well in soup and gravy. Again, prepare the ground flower in a sauce pan and then add it the soup or gravy. If you've ever wondered what to do with bacon grease, now you have an answer. If your sauce calls for solids - mushrooms for example - add them after you strain the mixture and put it back in the sauce pan. For meat and fish, make the butter sauce and brush it on either while the food is cooking or serve it in a gravy boat. The more fat in the meat, the more THC it will absorb. High heat will destroy much of the potency, so if you're looking for a high, add the sauce at the very end of the cooking process while the meat is resting. I've smoked dozens of racks of ribs with cannabutter in the final glaze. Lamb chops and venison are especially good meats for a cannabis sauce to temper the gaminess. Salad dressing has been epic fail. Yuk, is the only word that comes to mind. Cooked veggies take the flavors well. I've made Hollandaise sauce with cannabis that enhances asparagus. title: Material options for re-cladding of stair | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-43060127", "author_name": "Francesco", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-43060127", "date": "2022-12-06", "text": "Hi all, I have just removed an old carpet from my stair, revealing the basic MDF steps beneath. the flat is a council flat from the 80s, and it is likely that the stair was always meant to be carpeted. This is the main access stair to my flat, located on the first floor and with the front door on the ground floor. I would like to reclad the stair in timber and, with my basic DIY skills (but a keen interest in learning more about woodworking) I am thinking of doing this myself. This would be done by cladding the existing steps as I have seen in several tutorials, by glueing/nailing wood boards to the risers and goings. I am not keen to buy the prefabricated sets I have seen at B&Q etc because of their price and I am writing here to find other cost-effective alternatives. The flat has new engineered oak flooring throughout and the stair could match that. The flooring boards I used for the floor are 150mm wide and of varying lengths so I am not too convinced about using them to do the stair as it would look a bit patchy. Having had a look online, solid oak boards are quite expensive so I was wondering whether a veneered MDF with 0.5mm real oak veneer on either side could be a suitable alternative, but I am wondering how hard-wearing this would be? There is an option for oak edging as well. I also looked at pine boards, although they are generally sold in widths narrower than my goings (i.e. less than 280mm), except when buying a 'cill' or 'shelf' board.  The pine could be stained to look like oak, or alternatively, I could paint it in a solid colour which is something I would be happy to consider from a design standpoint. I have also seen plywood stairs online, but I wonder how suitable this would be for a stair that would be used daily. If I were to use plywood I might opt for hardwood plywood or marine plywood and possibly paint it and further treat it. Any thoughts or tips on the above, or other alternatives? We don\u2019t have an unlimited budget, so we\u2019re trying to identify the most bang for our buck by identifying low hanging fruit with big returns, so to speak.  We also plan to live here for somewhere between 2 to 7 years (but potentially longer if upsizing is impossible), so we have a dual purpose of improving quality of life for a family of 4 in a 2 bedroom, as well as maximising the eventual resale value of the condo. Here is the existing condition, along with a few constraints highlighted:   We\u2019ve spoken to a few structural engineers, and are preparing to finalise their scope of work and select a quote. The consensus seems to be that the electrical panel will be a costly endeavour to relocate, and that the galley wall, if removed, would require a post beneath the flush beam in the ceiling which extends from the bedroom wall. But the galley wall can be removed up until the flush beam without need for reinforcement. Given that, it seems the little corner may as well stay in place\u2026but on its own, it\u2019s an awkward relic. So my layout options so far surround with either counters or cabinetry.  Engineers have also confirmed the small bedroom could get a new door off the living room, but it\u2019s a load bearing wall so we definitely need to balance the cost/benefit of what would be additional costs of engineering, contractors and permitting. Some other notes, thoughts, constraints, questions : -Top priority is to open up and expand the kitchen; -Secondary objective is to improve the resale value, keep costs low, improve the dining space; -Tertiary goals are to improve the foyer (which currently had no place for shoes or coats) and add some storage (pantry, off-season closets, stroller parking, etc.) these would be nice to have, but we may have to make compromises. -We strongly prefer not to have a hood in the middle of the room (ie. over an island/peninsula). The existing hood fan is ductless, and ducting is not an option, so the eventual cooktop or range can go anywhere. -We are shopping around for 2nd hand appliances, and lean towards having a bigger fridge, but also counter depth, so we probably need to stick with 36\u201d wide. main_question: {"author_id": "aka-catherinet", "author_name": "catherinet (5IN)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/aka-catherinet", "date": "2022-12-07", "text": "My 4 burner electric stove is getting pretty old (25 years).  It has a big and a small element in the front and same in the back.  But the ones on the left side of the stove hardly ever get used, because they are too close to things I store on the counter right next to it.  I've noticed that the elements on the right (that get used all the time) are actually getting too hot, even at low settings.  Would it work better if I exchanged the elements from the less-used side of the stove to the right side?  Or is the problem with something else?  Thanks for your help.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "rwiegand", "author_name": "rwiegand", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rwiegand", "date": "2022-12-07", "text": "The elements are just big resistors, and their typical failure mode is to stop getting hot for a variety of reasons. Not much else can go wrong with them. By \"too hot\" do you mean that they are hotter than you've come to expect for a given setting, or that they are getting hotter than they've ever been? In either event the most likely culprit is the rheostat that changes the temperature as you turn the knob (if there are some kind of electronic controls then there are more possibilities). The likely cure is to replace the switches behind the knobs. In answer to your question, swapping the elements will probably make no difference. Swapping the controllers might. If the burners are getting much hotter than they've ever been I'd definitely call a repair person, you could have bumped up voltage from a defective transformer for example-- I'd expect to see other problems in the house were that the case, extra bright incandescent light bulbs, etc. A bum controller is the most likely cause.", "images": []}}

title: Worktop seam placement advice | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rebecca-__perkins", "author_name": "R P", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rebecca-__perkins", "date": "2022-12-07", "text": "Hi, I had my worktops templated for white quartz worktops in my new kitchen. It's a small kitchen and I'm having second thoughts about the seam placement. The fitter templating was very good. He said he would have preferred the seam to the right of the sink to be next to the hob and the sink piece to be one long piece running to the wall. This was not possible as they need 5cm between the hob cutout and the seam. I could move the hob 2cm to the right to achieve this but my extractor wouldn't be centered and I would lose a bit of the tiny space to the right of the hob where I could put pans. Have I made the right decision or should I have moved the hob over? Will the seam be horribly noticeable? (The extractor is concealed in a cupboard). To the right of the hob is a tall cabinet housing the oven.Any help is much appreciated. Thanks Becky", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/dd619081039120fd_5552-w500-h1000-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "lifestyle-kitchens-pfvwgb-pf~1385883894", "author_name": "Lifestyle Kitchens", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/kitchen-designers-and-remodelers/lifestyle-kitchens-pfvwgb-pf~1385883894", "date": "2022-12-08", "text": "You have made the right choice, especially if you have a seating area on the peninsular, if the hob was off centre to the extractor it would allways be noticeable everytime you sat down. how visible the joint is will be down to the colour of the quartz and how good the template/fitting is, if its just a solid white colour [without marble veins] and a small [2mm ish] gap and a colour matched jointing compound then it will look fine, anything with a vein the joints always look more prominent as the vein changes direction. The only other way i can see to do this [depends on the sizes and cost though] would be to make the sink and hob piece as one large L section [without a joint] or even if the hob wall piece is to wide to come out of the slab then i have had the joint run through the middle of the hob and as long as the joint is supported underneath i haven't had any problems. doing this does mean you have a small internal radius on the L section so i'd specify to do the same to the left of the sink as this would normally be a butt joint so the 2 internal corners would look the same.", "images": []}}

That will give you your diameter.  Then, I'd  measure exactly halfway along that measurement and put a piece of tape or other marking. Let's call that spot X.  Then, from X, you can measure a half-diameter in any direction.  That is the size of your rug.  You probably do want to take a bit of string of the half-diameter length and draw a circle to see where the rug will be under your chair. If the walls behind the chair are not the same size, you probably want to use the shorter.  For example, if one wall is 11 feet long and the other 10, you'd want to measure your diagonal from the edge of the 10 foot wall to 10 feet from the corner of the 11 foot wall. A circle enscribed in a square (ie the run inside the square made by the two walls behind the chair and 2 imaginary walls for the rest of the square) will have a diameter that is the diagonal measurement of the square (top right corner to bottom left corner). You can also do the whole thing with math with Pythagorus's theorem.  (A^2 + B^2 = C^2) Measure the shorter wall, square that (A^2), double it (this is B^2, but A=B), then take the square root for your diameter. Pay attention to any obstacles, like baseboards, radiators or other things.  You need to measure at the floor. If you want a bigger rug than the one that fits into your corner, you need to find a diagonal further into your room to measure, projecting from the walls. For example, a point midway into the door to an equal distance along the wall with the window. Since a circle enscribed in a square has the diameter of the diagonal of the square, as long as you have a square of floor space, you can figure out the diameter of the rug.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "webuser-616245866", "author_name": "Erica P", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-616245866", "date": "2022-12-08", "text": "This is 200 cm wide long way I\u2019m shooting for 200 cm diameter rug- thoughts?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b37268de039201f3_3297-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Rewiring a coach light | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "sgalen", "author_name": "Susie .", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sgalen", "date": "2022-12-08", "text": "We have four of these lights and three of them recently stopped working. Electrician came out and said that the wiring is corroded in the fixture. He thinks water got into the J-shaped conduit and caused it. He wasn't able to rewire them because the corrosion in the pipe blocked the wires. I hate to have to replace the lights - they're on the expensive end and would have to replace all four. Any ideas of how to clean out the corrosion so I can tunnel wires through?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/57b27e410392340c_5964-w500-h633-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-867564120", "author_name": "HU-867564120", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-867564120", "date": "2022-12-12", "text": "If the corrosion is as bad as you say, you'll need to get serious to rehabilitate the fixtures. The J tubes are likely steel tubing (inexpensive material & easy to form) so the corrosion is probably good old iron oxide. I would: - Disassemble the fixtures (cut wires as necessary) and get the J tubes out and separate. - Pour/dribble/soak CLR rust remover down through the tubes to eat away the rust. Mechanically assist the CLR to work its way through from both ends of the tube. This all may take soaking overnight, rinsing out depleted CLR and repeated applications of new CLR application. - When the old wire finally comes out, clean the tube ID as best you can, rinse and dry. - Repaint the J tubes and reassemble the fixture.", "images": []}}

So, why do grapes have sunburn symptoms? 1. Local Water Shortage: l The fruit is under the high temperature condition without shade of leaves l Leaves with high osmotic pressure compete for water from fruits with low osmotic pressure The above reasons can be obtained that, the grapes are partially dehydrated and finally sunburned. 2. Uneven Fertilization: Uneven fertilization ->unbalanced root nutrition of grape plants ->poor growth and tree vigor of grapes ->small and few leaves ->reduced resistance to sunlight ->fruit burns 3. Fruit Bagging Time Error: When bagging time is too late or the temperature is too high, it will aggravate sunburn. 4. title: It's raining!  IT'S RAINING!! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2022-12-09", "text": "Glory hallelujah, water is falling from the skies.  After a year and counting of seriously low precipitation, recently we received two inches of rain, and look on track to get another inch with the current front.  Southerners on here won't appreciate this at its worth, but I bet the Californians and Italians get it fine.  The reservoir, from being perilously close to empty, is just starting to fill.  To my more immediate satisfaction, the three days of planting I just completed are now getting the watering I was counting on given the forecast.  All very satisfactory. I haven't been posting much recently because I haven't had anything to say about roses, and don't know how much general garden talk the rose forum will bear.  But I shall now update. For several years now I've been working to a considerable extent on foundation plantings.  At the beginning of my gardening here at the farm I got enthusiastically launched on planting roses on a steep featureless slope, \"featureless\" meaning unfurnished with trees, shrubs, natural or manmade structures; also planting roses in ground that was much worse than I realized, much more inhospitable to roses.  After several years of the garden looking like a mess, and the world getting hotter and hotter, I decided I needed a lot of hedges and a lot of trees.  The idea was to plant thickly, so that the plants could protect each other, and so that they could furnish more organic matter to the garden; to plant higher hedges to provide visual barriers and boundaries, and barriers to wind and sun; to plant low hedges to mark the edges of beds and protect the feet of the roses.  Plants do more than this, of course.  They're important for water control, anchoring the ground with their roots (we live in a slide-prone area), rendering the soil more permeable, absorbing rainfall. So I've been planting hedges and trees for years, aiming at quantity over individually interesting plants, though a few of these do find their way in.  Privet, photinia, eleagnus 'Ebbingi', bay laurel, box (though box moth has been a plague); for low hedges phlomis (a champion), Mexican sage, rosemary, shrub germander (Teucrium fruticans).  The commonest trees are the Italian cypresses that define the main walk down the garden and form clumps here and there, then numberless flowering ashes and deciduous oaks.  This last week I planted a line of laburnums, wonderful multi-trunked small trees, as beautiful as they are tough, three checker trees (Sorbus torminalis), and two hazelnuts, hopeful that this last will survive and thrive now that I've finally figured out that it likes to grow along watercourses.  All three are native, the checker tree not overly common. And the roses?  Many aren't doing that well.  It doesn't help that, of the last six years, two have been droughty, not a good thing in an unwatered garden on a steep sunny southwest-facing slope. I dug up and replanted a couple of Chinas that were on the point of death, in the area where I've been working this fall, and was appalled by how bad the soil was.  One thing I have learned in twenty years of gardening here:  the theory that I've heard a few times, that it's best not to improve the soil before planting, is bunk.  No.  It doesn't improve by itself, at least not inevitably.  I've been digging recently in soil that has been left in grass and weeds since we got here, and an inch below the surface it's still pure gray clay, grading to sedimentary rock.  These planting holes were originally amended, but clearly inadequately. I think that, once we've gotten most of the foundation planting under control, I'll return to giving the roses more attention; and when I do, I'll be digging big holes and amending them drastically.  I hope to get around to the roses in a year or two.  Meanwhile, the garden is getting attention and new plants, and, now twenty years old, parts of it are, at moments, beautiful.", "images": []}

title: Rénovation radicale dans le 6ème arrondissement | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "leonore-grec-pfvwfr-pf~1296038965", "author_name": "Leonore Grec", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-architects/leonore-grec-pfvwfr-pf~1296038965", "date": "2022-12-09", "text": "Dans cet appartement au dernier \u00e9tage d\u2019un bel immeuble du 6\u00e8me arrondissement, la propri\u00e9taire ach\u00e8te son coup de c\u0153ur tout en d\u00e9plorant le petit s\u00e9jour ouvert sur la cuisine et le manque de rangements. Souhaitant inscrire une ambiance contemporaine \u00e0 son int\u00e9rieur, la propri\u00e9taire fait appel \u00e0 LG.archi qui l\u2019aide \u00e0 composer avec ses nombreux meubles anciens (bureau et commode en noyer, secr\u00e9taire marquet\u00e9 en acajou et suspension \u00e0 pampilles). L\u2019appartement est en tr\u00e8s bon \u00e9tat, r\u00e9nov\u00e9 r\u00e9cemment, il ne s\u2019agissait donc pas de tout d\u00e9molir\u2026 Entr\u00e9e, salon et chambres ont \u00e9t\u00e9 totalement r\u00e9nov\u00e9s ; cuisine et salle de bain ont \u00e9t\u00e9 seulement am\u00e9lior\u00e9es (placard et \u00e9tag\u00e8res suppl\u00e9mentaires, banc, portes de placard).     ENTR\u00c9E Pour mettre en valeur l\u2019entr\u00e9e aux volumes biscornus, LG.archi propose un papier peint Arte Walls qui enveloppe l\u2019espace et court jusque dans le couloir, et dont la tonalit\u00e9 principale \u00ab terre battue \u00bb est choisie pour une propri\u00e9taire fille de joueur de tennis. Le secr\u00e9taire \u00e0 jambes hautes du XVIII\u00e8me si\u00e8cle pose le d\u00e9cor d\u00e8s l\u2019entr\u00e9e, un geste esth\u00e9tique \u00ab utile \u00bb car il peut \u00eatre utilis\u00e9 en bureau d\u2019appoint dans une entr\u00e9e auparavant moins optimale. B\u00e9n\u00e9ficiant de la lumi\u00e8re naturelle en provenance du salon, il ne manque plus qu\u2019une chaise pour pouvoir en profiter. Le mix-match d\u00e9co ancien/contemporain est donn\u00e9 dans cet espace au premier coup d\u2019\u0153il : gravure ancienne et appliques contemporaines couleur \u00ab or \u00bb, lustre \u00e0 pampilles et papier peint contemporain ; le service d\u00e9coration de LG.archi existe pour trouver les bonnes combinaisons de couleurs et de mat\u00e9riaux ! Pr\u00e8s de la porte d\u2019entr\u00e9e (pas de photo), un am\u00e9nagement sobre est choisi par contraste : les portes en plaqu\u00e9 bois du vestiaire ont \u00e9t\u00e9 remplac\u00e9es par des portes en bois peint en blanc et l\u2019int\u00e9rieur du meuble a \u00e9t\u00e9 modifi\u00e9 pour davantage de fonctionnalit\u00e9s (pouvoir ranger une planche \u00e0 repasser, int\u00e9grer une tringle t\u00e9lescopique en partie haute). LG.archi conseille aussi sur des questions purement fonctionnelles !     SALON et CUISINE Le parquet est conserv\u00e9 dans les parties de r\u00e9ception de l\u2019appartement : entr\u00e9e, salon et cuisine. Un claustra en noyer a \u00e9t\u00e9 pens\u00e9 sur mesure par LG.archi et ajout\u00e9 comme s\u00e9paratif entre le salon et la cuisine, sans cacher la lumi\u00e8re naturelle lorsqu\u2019on cuisine. Le salon, muni d\u2019une seule fen\u00eatre, s\u2019est \u00e9toff\u00e9 en rangements dans les moindres recoins : une biblioth\u00e8que int\u00e8gre un mur en saillie existant et un meuble de rangements se niche dans la sous-pente _auparavant place perdue et difficilement am\u00e9nageable_. Les meubles en bois peint s\u2019int\u00e8grent parfaitement \u00e0 l\u2019espace, comme s\u2019ils avaient toujours \u00e9t\u00e9 l\u00e0 _gr\u00e2ce \u00e0 la corniche de finition ajout\u00e9e_, et gr\u00e2ce au soin apport\u00e9 dans les d\u00e9tails de mise en oeuvre. Rigueur, alignement et proportion sont ici les ma\u00eetres-mots du projet. Au centre de la biblioth\u00e8que, la TV-cadre \u00e9tait souhait\u00e9e par la propri\u00e9taire ; LG.archi propose alors de fausses portes de placard agenc\u00e9es sous la TV, de mani\u00e8re \u00e0 int\u00e9grer la saillie existante \u00e0 la nouvelle biblioth\u00e8que et d\u2019att\u00e9nuer la pr\u00e9sence de la TV dans le salon. Des tringles \u00e0 rideaux, cintr\u00e9es, en m\u00e9tal fonc\u00e9, ont \u00e9t\u00e9 pens\u00e9es int\u00e9gralement pour les lieux gr\u00e2ce \u00e0 Ireale Tapissier et un syst\u00e8me d\u2019accroche ing\u00e9nieux \u00e9tait n\u00e9cessaire pour le mur en sous-pente. De magnifiques rideaux en lin clair dot\u00e9s d\u2019une passementerie \u00ab orang\u00e9e-rouge \u00bb ont \u00e9t\u00e9 con\u00e7us sur mesure et mont\u00e9s sur des anneaux en m\u00e9tal ; ils habillent d\u00e9sormais de mani\u00e8re \u00e9l\u00e9gante ce salon ! De magnifiques coussins lumineux de chez Trendethics compl\u00e8tent la d\u00e9coration !     Le tapis Pierre Frey -\u00e9galement con\u00e7u sur mesure- finalise en beaut\u00e9 la d\u00e9coration de ce salon ; les canap\u00e9s, fauteuils et pouf reprennent les tons chaleureux chers \u00e0 la propri\u00e9taire. Le buffet en noyer massif du XIX\u00e8me s\u2019int\u00e8gre d\u00e9sormais \u00e0 l\u2019am\u00e9nagement int\u00e9rieur sans alourdir le reste, et rappelle la teinte du claustra en noyer. La cuisine est conserv\u00e9e ouverte sur le salon tout en ayant une touche d\u00e9corative plus ad\u00e9quate \u00e0 la nouvelle ambiance du salon aux tons \u00e9cru et \u00ab terre battue \u00bb. Des portes en plaqu\u00e9-bois sur les meubles hauts de la cuisine ont \u00e9t\u00e9 remplac\u00e9es par des portes Plum en cannage couleur Terracota, toujours dans un souci d\u2019harmonie des couleurs. Les suspensions ont \u00e9t\u00e9 supprim\u00e9es pour d\u00e9gager le plafond qui \u00e9tait encombr\u00e9\u2026 finalement l\u2019\u00e9nergie circule beaucoup mieux dans la pi\u00e8ce ! COULOIR Dans le couloir, \u00e9troit et tr\u00e8s long (plus de 8m !), comment remplacer l\u2019ennui et la monotonie ? L\u2019id\u00e9e principale \u00e9tait de rendre vivant cet espace de passage, de le rendre agr\u00e9able et chaleureux au quotidien : l\u2019habillage du mur avec le papier peint Arte Walls et l\u2019installation d\u2019un grand mur de rangements transforment radicalement l\u2019espace sans empi\u00e9ter sur la largeur de passage n\u00e9cessaire. Ainsi, d\u2019un c\u00f4t\u00e9 une galerie des tableaux et de l\u2019autre, un mur couvert de souvenirs de voyage, d\u2019objets anciens ou de musique\u2026 l\u2019endroit parfait pour exposer ses collections personnelles ! La pr\u00e9fabrication du meuble sur mesure permet une pose rapide in situ en 2 ou 3 jours seulement, tout en int\u00e9grant les \u00e9l\u00e9ments existants contraignants (un radiateur et un compteur \u00e9lectrique) :  le tout s\u2019agence parfaitement et on ne voit plus les \u00e9l\u00e9ments disgracieux totalement int\u00e9gr\u00e9s au reste ! D\u00e9sormais, le couloir devient un v\u00e9ritable cabinet de curiosit\u00e9s, o\u00f9 l\u2019on prend plaisir \u00e0 s\u2019attarder\u2026 La moquette au sol peaufine l\u2019aspect \u00ab cosy \u00bb de cette zone \u00ab nuit \u00bb de l\u2019appartement, \u00e0 contrario du parquet moins salissant dans les zones \u00ab jour \u00bb (entr\u00e9e, salon, cuisine).     SALLE DE BAIN Dans la salle de bain d\u00e9j\u00e0 r\u00e9nov\u00e9e, LG.archi propose des micro-interventions pour am\u00e9liorer le confort de l\u2019espace et satisfaire la propri\u00e9taire : un banc sur mesure est ajout\u00e9 dans la douche, et un placard toute hauteur s\u2019ins\u00e8re entre la douche et le meuble vasque. Trait\u00e9 pour recevoir de l\u2019eau en grande quantit\u00e9, le banc en bambou constitue la touche d\u00e9co id\u00e9ale et pratique pour se savonner, faire des gommages ou se couper les ongles de pied ! Sous la grande vasque, le tiroir de rangement n\u2019\u00e9tait pas suffisant pour la propri\u00e9taire, l\u2019id\u00e9e du meuble toute hauteur optimise ce coin perdu sans effet de masse et en harmonie avec les mat\u00e9riaux existants ! Le c\u00f4t\u00e9 lisse du placard contraste tr\u00e8s bien avec le rev\u00eatement mural tr\u00e8s pr\u00e9sent, et les portes battantes s\u2019ouvrent discr\u00e8tement dans le d\u00e9cor. Ainsi l\u2019espace est plus confortable et LG.archi a r\u00e9ussi \u00e0 pr\u00e9server un espace r\u00e9cemment r\u00e9nov\u00e9 par des interventions fines sans exc\u00e8s de z\u00e8le ! Le tout para\u00eet plus lumineux et mieux agenc\u00e9 pour le bonheur de la propri\u00e9taire.     CHAMBRE 1 Dans la chambre d\u2019ami \u00e0 l\u2019univers froid et sans \u00e2me, LG.archi pense un dressing enti\u00e8rement sur mesure pour s\u2019adapter \u00e0 un volume existant peu heureux et modifie les placards existants par des \u00e9tag\u00e8res ouvertes et discr\u00e8tes. Des portes en cannage et une alc\u00f4ve rouge flash (laissant la possibilit\u00e9 d\u2019installer un canap\u00e9-lit) r\u00e9chauffent grandement l\u2019atmosph\u00e8re ! Des d\u00e9tails comme les poign\u00e9es en bois apportent aussi une tonalit\u00e9 naturelle et chaleureuse. Dans la sous-pente, des \u00e9tag\u00e8res ouvertes compl\u00e8tent les rangements en optimisant l\u2019espace. Sur le mur, pr\u00e8s de la fen\u00eatre, un radiateur extra-plat remplace le radiateur existant qui se trouvait sous la fen\u00eatre, tout en facilitant la manutention des rideaux. Remarquez cette magnifique toile de jouy de chez Casal pour les rideaux, et ce, toujours dans un souci d\u2019\u00e9gayer la pi\u00e8ce en rappelant le fil \u00ab rouge terre battue \u00bb du projet ! Notez \u00e9galement l\u2019abat-jour renvers\u00e9 en guise de suspension et sa bordure... La moquette claire contraste avec le reste, pour rendre l\u2019espace plus cosy. Et toujours ces superbes coussins Trendethics ! L\u2019ensemble fonctionne bien et l\u2019ambiance est beaucoup plus lumineuse !         CHAMBRE 2 Dans la chambre principale, tout a \u00e9t\u00e9 repens\u00e9 : la t\u00eate de lit sur mesure, les placards, le rev\u00eatement de sol, les rideaux, la suspension et le radiateur. Le mur en saillie existant est \u00e0 nouveau englob\u00e9 dans le nouveau meuble t\u00eate de lit pens\u00e9 sur mesure par LG.archi. Les tonalit\u00e9s beiges des nouveaux agencements contrastent avec le blanc du mur, tout en \u00e9l\u00e9gance. L\u2019ambiance \u00ab bureau \u00bb de cette pi\u00e8ce n\u2019est plus qu\u2019un p\u00e2le souvenir ; d\u00e9sormais des rideaux en velours Terracota de chez Pierre Frey dynamisent les tons plus clairs. You can purchase them already formulated and bagged (much like the Nutriboost product) but those tend to be overly pricey for what you get. main_question: {"author_id": "jerry-hsieh69", "author_name": "Coffee Nut", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jerry-hsieh69", "date": "2022-12-10", "text": "Hi all, we are Doing a new build and would really like to use large format slams in our master bathroom. Our shower wall is 6.5\u2019 + 5\u2019 long with 9\u2019 ceilings. We got some really nice pricing for our slab at $16 per square feet which comes out to be around $2K in materials. Our builder came back with a quote for $11K For the shower only. Is this reasonable? I get that these large format slabs are more difficult to install, but I was surprised by the quote, and there is no transparency on breaking down what is material versus labor. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~687879239", "author_name": "Dragonfly Tile & Stone Works, Inc.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~687879239", "date": "2022-12-11", "text": "The cost is not unreasonable, and actually sounds low for installation of that material. .  The price of the panels is minor compared to the installation materials and labor. The cost of STANDARD  tile is also minor compared to labor and materials for a properly built shower.   It IS more expensive to install GPTP (Gauged Porcelain Tile Panels) as qualified contractors must be properly trained and have the equipment. The industry (both professional trade organizations and manufacturers) have training programs (usually 2-5 day programs) for contractors to get proper training and certification in GPTP installation.  Hopefully your contractor is aware of the installation requirements. They are not installaed by one person, but by a team of installers.  To give you (and others who responded here) a bit of perspective about the training required: \"Due to the extremely large modules that Gauged Porcelain Tile/Gauged Porcelain Tile Panels are available in, installation of this product is significantly different from the installation of standard large format porcelain tile, requiring special installation tools and techniques.  The unique installation procedures and workmanship considerations, are as outlined in ANSI A108.19 American National Standard Specifications for \"Interior Installation of Gauged Porcelain Tile and Gauged Porcelain Tile Panels/Slabs by the Thin-Bed Method bonded with Modified Dry-Set Cement Mortar or Improved Modified Dry-Set Cement Mortar\u201d.Some key issues addressed by ANSI A108.19 include: Contractor Qualifications Jobsite and Material Handling Requirements Substrate Flatness and General Requirements Floor and Wall Installation procedures for ANSI A137.3 Table 4 gauged products Wall Installation Procedures for ANSI A137.3 Table 5 gauged products Mortar, and Mortar Application Unique coverage criteria and evaluation procedures Lippage criteria and use of lippage control systems Special floor setting provisions that involve embedding by walking Movement Joints \" You can assume that a properly credentialed installation team is not concerned about the cost of one slab breaking and I would not suggest that you try to negotiate pricing by offering to \"eat it if they break it\".  In addition, the contractor (if qualified) will be responsible for transport of the slabs as they require specific equipment and handling procedures. You do NOT want to attempt this yourself as it can be quite dangerous.  Doubtful a supplier would even allow it. I hope this provides a little perspective on GTPT installation for consideration in shower pricing.  Good luck with your project.", "images": []}}

title: help with crown molding! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "anne-laporte", "author_name": "Anne LaPorte", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anne-laporte", "date": "2022-12-11", "text": "Can someone help? We thought we had to just do another 45 degree cut for the corners but it\u2019s not lining up.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5132c41f039665e8_0878-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8122c486039665e9_0878-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "w0lley32", "author_name": "w0lley32", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/w0lley32", "date": "2022-12-12", "text": "Like others have posted, you have to basically cut your molding upside down.  On your mitre saw, you have to position the portion of the crown molding that will be against the ceiling on the base of your mitre saw, and the portion of the crown molding that will be against the wall on the fence of your mitre saw.  Keep in mind that if you need to mitre the left of the molding, the mitre will be on your right on your saw.  Then you flip the molding over and it should line up, providing your corner is exactly 90 degrees.  Also, make sure you hold the piece of molding at exactly the same angle on your saw as it will lay on your wall.  For this, cut a small piece of molding about 1 foot long, and lay it against the corner of the ceiling and wall the way it should go, and make a mark on the ceiling and another one on the wall where the crown molding ends.  Remove the molding, and measure the distance, on the ceiling, between the corner and your mark.  Transpose that mark on the base of your mitre saw. For beginners, it can help to put a piece of painters tape on your fence and write \"wall\" and another piece on the table and write \"ceiling\".", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-187866520", "author_name": "Ingrid_vc zone 9b, San Diego Co. inland", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-187866520", "date": "2022-12-13", "text": "I've spent a pleasant few days visiting public gardens, most of them in England, both for the enjoyment of seeing many roses in many different situations, but after a while also paying attention to how the roses were grown and displayed.  Since I'm starting a brand new garden of my own, the gods and the ground squirrels willing, I'm paying attention to how what  I've seen and admired in public gardens can be translated to my at this point very modest little plot. I have to say that for me variety is the spice of life.  The gardens that had the most diversity in color, size, plant habit and height were the most enchanting to me.  Rows of roses, such as I saw in one or two sections of the David Austin rose garden in England, did not move me in the least, and this was especially true where there was little color variation.  Other parts of the garden that featured pergolas with climbing roses and ramblers, and roses that were old varieties rather than their home brand, which had a much greater variation in bloom and plant size, were the most pleasing to me. The roses I've planted or ordered include pinks, purples, white and yellows so I seem to be pretty well covered in the color department, except for red roses which I don't care for.  I have one climber (Lamarque) and one very tall rose (Aloha) and the remainder range from short to medium tall, which hopefully will provide the diversity in height that I want.  Flower size also ranges from small (Aunt Margy's Rose, Lauren, International Herald Tribune) to quite large (Aloha).  I'd love to also have companion plants again but those were the first thing to be eaten by the ground squirrels in my previous garden, before they went on to the roses. title: A Delicious (IMO!) New Salmon Dish I Discovered and Wanted to Share | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lynnnm", "author_name": "LynnNM", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lynnnm", "date": "2022-12-14", "text": "*And, if it doesn't sound good or interesting to you personally, PLEASE  just pass on by without negative comments!  SPICY SALMON, NORI & RICE BOWLS 6 Servings ** NOTES before you start: ~ When I came across the recipe, there was no indication as to what to bake it in other than \u201cmuffin slots\u201d. First try was putting them in a metal muffin pan, but this made it very messy to try and pull them out and plate them in one nice-looking serving! I would suggest using six individual 4-ounce ceramic baking cups/ramekins. Or, perhaps using just 3-4 of the 8-ounce ones and just dividing the nori, then the salmon between them before baking. Serving them in the dishes at the table. ~ This sauce is a MUST! It absolutely makes the dish so delicious. ~ If unfamiliar with Nori, it is thin sheets of an edible, tasty & very healthful dried seaweed. ~ \u201cSushi Rice\u201d is a short-grain Japanese rice. These days often sold as just \u201dSushi Rice\u201d. If you can\u2019t find any then long-grain California white rice is a passable substitute. Do NOT use the kinds of rice used for curry or burritos, though! ~ Sriracha Sauce comes in a bottle like soy sauce and can usually be found in most grocery stores, either with the Asian bottled sauces or International bottled sauces. Ingredients: \u00a8 2 sheets Nori paper, cut with scissors into 4 equal squares each. \u00a8  3/4 cup cooked sushi rice, cooled Ingredients for the Salmon: \u00a8 1/2 lb. fresh salmon, skin removed, cut into approx. 1/2\u201d cubes \u00a8 1 TBS sesame (or olive) oil \u00a8 1/2 TBS soy sauce \u00a8 1/2 TBS honey \u00a8 1 scallion, sliced crosswise \u00a8 1/4 tsp each of garlic powder, onion powder, chili powder, paprika, dried oregano, & salt. Ingredients for the Sauce: \u00a8 1/4 cup mayo (Kewpie brand if you have it) \u00a8 2 tsp Sriracha sauce \u00a8 1 tsp honey Toppings: \u00a8 1/2 avocado, diced small \u00a8 1 tsp black sesame seeds Directions: 1) Preheat your oven to 400-degrees F. 2) Place your cubed salmon into a bowl with all the rest of the salmon ingredients and toss gently to coat well. Marinate for 15 minutes (or up to 4 hours). 3) Cook up your sushi rice, if not already done. Let cool. 4) Make up the Spicy Sauce and set aside until time to serve. 5) After your salmon has marinated, put together the individual bowls like this: 6) On your counter, lay out a sheet of waxed paper to work on. Next lay your nori squares down onto it. Divide your cooked and cooled rice in a mound on the middle of each square. The moisture from the rice will quickly start to soften the nori, making it then easier to nestle them into each ramekin. ** If using the larger baking dishes, overlap 2 nori squares and then add the rice. 7) With a thin, very lightly oiled spatula quickly pick up the riced squares and nestle each into a ramekin. Divide the now marinated diced salmon, placing them over the rice. 8) Place the ramekins onto a sturdy baking/cookie sheet. Bake for 15-17 minutes. You can broil them afterwards for 1-2 minutes if crisping up the salmon more is desired. 9) Serve individual ramekins on plates, topping each with the diced avocado. Drizzle with the Spicy Sauce and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Serve rest of this delicious sauce at the table.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/58d2f4aa03991239_6057-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

Would it be too dark? What our contractor is doing: removing the bathtub, and making that the area where you walk into the shower. So where the tub is now will just be flooring, and the shower opening will face two windows (one north-facing, one west-facing) and the vanity lighting that's above our mirrors. That also means, where the glass door to the shower is now will be a wall. The wall won't go all the way up to the ceiling. Why we're redoing it: Our current shower lacks built-in storage, so we've been using that metal shower caddy in the photo. The grout at the bottom, near the shower pan is old and gross. And we don't need a bathtub in our master since there are two other tubs in this house. Other details: we're repainting the walls, adding new light fixtures, new faucets, shower head, new floor tile will extend into walk-in closet and water closet (potentially heated, not sure if it's worth it). Here's the room:     I can provide more images in the comments below if needed. Another reason for the wall (instead of glass surround): Adding a shower niche for storage might not be doable with glass. Why? Because building a niche into the wall that faces the outside of the house will mean removing insulation. So the wall that separates our shower from the cold Colorado air would suddenly become much thinner. Having a wall (instead of a glass surround) would mean we could attach shower storage to the inside of the shower wall without it cutting into insulation. My gut feeling: A glass surround would let more light into the shower and it's what appears to be most \"on-trend\" but I'm worried that functionally, it'll lead to the same problem we started with: lack of storage, having to squeegee glass every day, and visible shower products and loofahs. One last question: Adding a wall will mean making the shower a little narrower. Because walls are thicker than glass. So how narrow can a three-walled shower be without causing discomfort? I'll want to wash my hair without hitting my elbows on the walls but I realize that reaching your head doesn't require your elbow-span to be fully out to the sides. (This is such a weird thing to ask!) In fact, I leave salt out of a lot of recipes because I often have an aversion to it. What are your favorite things to eat that fit in with low carb and low salt? My sister just sent us a Christmas package that has a lot of candy in it but also half a dozen pears from Oregon.  I know the candy is bad, but what about the pears?  Are they high in carbohydrates? It is easy for me to cut out salt, but carbs are another matter.  For that matter, my sodium levels are already low. I really like grains and pasta and have found it next to impossible to cut these out, and so I am looking for ways to make them fit in with my diet.  The doctor also told me to have a low fat diet, but I will not take that to an extreme, as I know that many nutrients are fat soluble and that a certain amount of fat is necessary to help make one feel full and stop eating. I also like potatoes and like them without salt or sour cream, but I do like a bit of butter.  I also like to make potato frittatas with eggs, cheese, and peppers. main_question: {"author_id": "paul-griffin4728", "author_name": "Paul Griffin", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/paul-griffin4728", "date": "2022-12-14", "text": "Looking for some advise on the best way to rub my system, live on the eastern coast of Canada so it\u2019s a cold high precipitation environment. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-159402497", "author_name": "HU-159402497", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-159402497", "date": "2022-12-15", "text": "I moved into a new construction home on 1/2 acre lot. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "callirhoe123", "author_name": "callirhoe123", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/callirhoe123", "date": "2022-12-15", "text": "What you want is organic matter, any you can find and dig into the soil.  Compost, leaves, grass clippings etc.  What ever is available in your area.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "jlhart76", "author_name": "jlhart76", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jlhart76", "date": "2022-12-15", "text": "We moved to OKC in 2015 & I got my first real experience with clay soil. First off, clay isn't the horrible monster everyone acts like it is. Clay is normally super high in nutrients, you just have to get it to a usable form. Right now, I'd give anything for a truck load of clay soil, I prefer it over this sandbox of a yard I have now. Most soil particles are like wadded up pieces of paper. Piled together, they still have little pockets of air between them. Clay is more like a ream of paper. The particles are flat sheets, so they stick together & don't allow air between them. Var. glauca is easy to identify: look for highly reflexed bracts. Var. menziesii is trickier. From images I have seen on Inaturlist and other sites, it's evident that not all glauca have obviously reflexed bracts; some are straight and even--though rarely--appressed. This seems more common with var. glauca located between B.C.'s Cascades and Rocky Mountains (this owing to the fact that it intergrades with var. menziesii, which occupies the west/south west portion of this range). The problem, though, is number. Photos show only so many cones, and I've noticed that some local trees will produce cones that in a small sample size seem to have straight bracts, but when collected in a sufficient quantity will reveal a trend toward the reflexed. In summary: a certain level of bract reflexion will confirm var. glauca but no bract positioning will confirm var. menziesii. We have a pretty simple white and gold kitchen (the new undermount sink will be stainless and we are doing a gold faucet to match the cabinet pulls) so it felt like the countertops could handle a bevel without it being one of the more overly ornate edges. Bevel edge:    2) The template guy said more radius for the corners is better to prevent chips, but I like the more squared off look. There seems to not be the best standardization between fabricators on naming, but all the 'eased' square radius options online have a little roundness so its never a true 90 degree corner. Our current laminate has huge rounded corners and he showed me a little plastic overlay of the smaller rounded radius he suggested & it was a great improvement from what we have. Then I see pics like below and love the clean square corners! It feels more modern (though a Google search claims rounded edges are 'in'??? to me its the opposite - the more round and bulbous the more dated it would be?).   We have decent room around our island compared to other homes we have been in where the island is more cramped, so I'm not super worried about hitting corners. Don't remember ever hitting myself on previous islands or peninsulas. Can I get opinions on: 1) whether prioritizing defense against possible chips is more important to you than the corner radius aesthetic & your experiences with quartz chipping at the corners?
