title: Floorplan advice on kitchen and house remodel | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-897771785", "author_name": "BC Jones", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-897771785", "date": "2022-12-16", "text": "Hello - This post is now edited for more clarity.  I already have worked with some KDs at cabinet vendors, and have had pro contractors look at the house overall and offered rough advice (\"you can build here and there for this much,\" etc.) that has informed these plans here.  I have some local advice resources as well. I was hoping to see if the community here has better ideas about specific aspects that I can use to inform my next conversations with pros.  I am under no illusions that I can cowboy everything.  For more detail about us as residents of this house, I wrote a response in the comments, how old we are, kids, how we live, etc. This is in the SF Bay Area, where all costs are high. For most people, including us, it's too expensive to just find a better house nearby; the jumps between quality tiers are too big, and supply is too small.  So I have to focus on bang for the buck, and part of that is minimizing the disturbance of existing space, and which also enables us to live in the house through almost all of the work.  Prefer to keep the rear yard intact also - another reason for confining work to the West side of the parcel.  Prefer to not add any more square feet than we need to. I'm asking for feedback on the plan for the kitchen remodel part (construction mid-2023), and also feedback on the second phase, the larger project, which should be done in a 2 or 3 yrs and consist of an addition over the garage (not shown, just stairs shown).   Esthetics:  currently very slight mid-century modern.  We both like modern, and want to go in that direction. First photo below is the kitchen and house as-is.  Second photo is one new plan (with a 4th BR), and the third is a second new plan (with a family room instead of 4th BR).   The kitchen in photos 2 and 3 are the same - the proposed new kitchen. House as-is is in the first photo below.  All of these are close-to-scale.  This first image is graph paper, the following 2 are tracing paper on top of the graph paper, so the proportions should be close to correct.  The below photos are prospective. New kitchen is the same in the below photos.  Don't think that the table size and placement are locked - I could do a banquette in approx the same place as the table on the left/East side, opening up more walking space on the right.  I think the space could work with a 3-ft wide table. Other than the kitchen, the below images show 2 different ideas for the rest of the house: Create a private 4th br with separated access:  Idea, probably better - create a family room, more light at the South end of the kitchen as well:    This last photo, from a cabinet vendor visit, does not show the island. The kitchen is near-original, 13 x 9 feet, in a 1949 3br 2ba 1300 sq ft ranch. The kitchen plan I've come up with (call it phase 1 of the work) does the following:  A.) Removes the wall separating the kitchen from the dining room, which we are using as an extension of the living room (We like the sense of a large space.) B.) Removes a section of that same wall that borders the adjacent living room.  This allows room for a 3x5 island with sufficient clearance.  The existing kitchen 'U' will be removed for the island.  Sink, refrigerator and range will stay in the same places.  The cave-feeling of the rear of the kitchen will be gone. I was thinking that this island should be non-seating for space reasons, but I'm not 100% sure.  We want the option of continuing to use the dining room as an extension of the living room, or maybe putting a table there someday.  The eventually-expanded kitchen (see below) will also have a table, and room for a decent-sized one. Any opinions on island size? 3x5 in the plan, but could be a little shorter than 5 feet to add more clearance at the South end.  It could be longer, too - but I'd rather not take down all of that East/left kitchen side wall - I'd rather still maintain some room separation. I considered not doing an island, but then the alternative to add work space is a peninsula maintaining the 'U', which I find really cramped. Or, annexing the dining room to the kitchen and rearranging the entire cabinet and appliance layout. (I don't see a benefit, plus more expensive.) Or, waiting until Phase 2 and adding a not-well-located cabinet against the wall across from the refrigerator to improve counter space, but that would be far from the work areas. If anyone has thoughts on the cabinet layout, great, though I learned a lot here and I think what I have can work. Phase 2 of the larger house plan (2-3 years from now) will involve removing the rear/South wall of the kitchen (yes, I know that between phase 1 and 2 the back of the kitchen will be cramped).  This will create a larger usable eat in kitchen, have good flow and allow egress to the backyard. This eliminates the poorly-placed 3rd bedroom, which will be added back with a new main suite above the garage (the single largest value-add - the house currently has no suite) plus an additional 4th bedroom (or family room).  The existing 1st and 2nd bedrooms and existing main bathroom, and most of the existing living and dining room won't be touched except floor and drywall patches/replacement. The new 4th bedroom or family room area is where I'd like to hear some opinions.  Check out the second (plan 2) and third (plan 3) images.  Having a 4th bedroom in plan 2 is a nice resale value-add, but it does not seem the most effective and esthetic use of space in the second image.  This plan has a new hallway created in the old garage area that connects the 4th to a new bathroom and the kitchen - it is more private.  Maybe too separated?   And it's complicated.  Might be more expensive due to extra walls and foundation area added? The third plan (plan 3) image shows that new rear room instead turned into a family room, and the new bathroom is connected directly with a cove so it doesn't open directly to the room.  Is there a better way to do this?  It's a 3 foot deep mini-hallway, figure the door would be 30 inches.   If anyone has suggestions on this bath and laundry combo, great - it's about 11 feet wide and 7 feet deep.  Figure bathroom as you walk in and laundry as you turn right.  Maybe I should do a different Houzz post on this one. Plan 3 has much nicer egress to rear, and could have large windows and doors.  And here is an add-on idea for the third plan: has anyone here seen anyone take a room like this and add a folding wall on tracks to give flexibility to using the space?   It could go where the wall in image 2 is.   As nice as it would be to have a family room, we already have a large living room.  I'd prefer to keep the new second story just the main suite, and not add another bedroom up there.   But this plan may just be easier and simpler. The first image is the house as-is.  The second image is plan 2, and shows the new kitchen as described above plus the addition  phase 2.   Third image is plan 3. 4th image is of the cabinet layout, minus the island (will have all drawers plus microwave open shelf.)   The cabinet to the right of the stove will be about 36 inches, all drawers.   Per measurements I might have an extra inch or three to play with, but not sure. title: Custom cabinets less expensive than semi-custom? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-918119203", "author_name": "HU-918119203", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-918119203", "date": "2022-12-17", "text": "I'm planning a complete renovation of my current U-shaped kitchen, including all-new cabinetry.  The renovated kitchen will be an L-shape plus an island open to the dining room and will have a large floor-to-ceiling pantry on the third wall, although it will remain relatively small (about 15x12).  My contractor got a quote for custom cabinets from a shop he trusts at around $30k.  (This is in Fairfield County, CT.)  With some other items coming in over budget, I decided to explore semi-stock cabinets.  My options were limited because inset cabinetry is non-negotiable (my house is historic), but I got some back-of-the-envelope quotes from Ring's End (I believe the Decora line) and Crown Point Cabinetry.  Both told me I'd be closer to $40k.  That surprised me, since I'd assumed custom was more expensive.  I asked the Ring's End rep why I'd pay more for semi-custom cabinets, and her only explanation was that the finish is more durable, there is a warranty, and a custom cabinet shop could pack up and leave town and I'd have no one to follow up with if there were issues (??). Is this consistent with what others are seeing?  My only real concern is that I'm being underquoted by the custom cabinet maker, but I do trust my contractor.  Otherwise, the supposed advantages of semi-custom cabinets are not that impressive for an extra $10k, particularly since with custom cabinets I can choose the exact paint shade and detailing that I want.", "images": []}

Die Trampelei von \u00fcber mir st\u00f6rt mich gar nicht so sehr, aber die Stimmen irritieren mich doch ziemlich. Es kommt von oben und von der Seite (ggf. ist das von oben doch der TV, da da meines Wissens nur 1 Person wohnt, aber ich h\u00f6re keinerlei Bassgewummer). Von oben kommt nur leichtes \"Gemurmel\", aber von der Seite kriege ich recht viel mit. Ich vermute, dass mein Schlafzimmer an ein Kinderzimmer oder Wohnzimmer angrenzt. Ich kann das Baby ab und zu leise weinen h\u00f6ren. Etwas lauter ist dann das Duziedu der Mutter (hohe Stimme). Und recht laut der Vater (tiefe durchdringende Stimme), der wohl gerne Monologe h\u00e4lt (oder telefoniert). main_question: {"author_id": "the-joy-of-blinds-and-shutters-pfvwgb-pf~378271292", "author_name": "The JOY of Blinds and Shutters", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/window-treatments/the-joy-of-blinds-and-shutters-pfvwgb-pf~378271292", "date": "2022-12-18", "text": "This is a common question, especially during the winter months. In the UK, ladybirds (or ladybugs) hibernate from December to March. They may also come into your home and hide in spaces that are cool and dark. In settling down for the winter, they aim for areas in your home that are as high as possible, e.g., the top of window frames and door frames. If you have blinds or shutters, ladybirds are often found huddled together at the very top of these products where the temperature is cooler than the atmosphere within the room. The first time you might see them is when you open your windows during the winter to help clear the condensation or to ventilate the room. You\u2019ll find them fast asleep in a little group. As they tend to crawl vertically until they find a cosy place for hibernation, you may also see them hiding within the hardware of blinds. If you find ladybirds within your home, if they\u2019re not in your way, you don\u2019t need to remove them as they\u2019ll sleep peacefully until the spring. As the weather gets warmer, they\u2019ll and leave your home of their own accord. If you\u2019ve disturbed them accidentally, just pop them into a dark area and they\u2019ll go back to sleep. Have you spotted ladybirds (or any other hibernating insects) at the top of your blinds or shutters? I look forward to hearing about your experiences! title: Weird happenings... Part II | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "anniedeighnaugh", "author_name": "Annie Deighnaugh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anniedeighnaugh", "date": "2022-12-20", "text": "Some of you may recall the weird goings on at our house from a couple of years ago. (https://www.gardenweb.com/discussions/5927960/now-this-is-weird-very-weird#n=81) Well, now we have more.... The other day, the painter was painting the family room, and DH and I were in the back talking and we heard this loud bang...really loud, like an explosion.  I thought something happened with the painter and ran out and asked if he was ok.  He was fine and thought something big fell in the library.  Well, we looked all over the house and could see nothing out of place.  The sound was from our level, but just in case, we check the lower level and the attic too and there was nothing that seemed off.  We looked at the gas fireplace and it was fine, the glass was fine and the pilot light was burning as usual.  Not a clue.  But I kept looking and finally got the flashlight to look at the fireplace more closely.  It seemed some of the fake logs were moved and up against the glass which was not normal....though DH says they look fine to him.  But we turned the pilot light off, and shut both gas valves just to be safe and are waiting for service to show up. My theory is that there was a small slow leak inside the unit.  As the gas is heavier than air, the bottom of the fireplace slowly filled up with gas until it filled up to the pilot light where it was ignited in a big explosion.  For some reason, it wasn't enough to blow out the pilot light.  What do I know, but it sort of sounds like a possibility to me. But then the next a.m. I go in to take a shower and there's a metal cover from the steam unit outlet in the shower that appears to have been blown across the shower and is sitting on the shower floor.  The cover seemed fine, and I put it back on the unit. It took sufficient effort to get it back on, so it's not like the cats could've played with it and knocked it out or anything.  And it certainly would require some force to blow it off across the shower.  But that unit has nothing to do with the gas fireplace.  It is electric only and it was off.  Even if it came on by itself somehow, it's not an explosive kind of thing.  And we checked downstairs in the closet where the unit is on the wall and it looks pristine. So now there's a real mystery....were the events connected though seemingly impossible they would be?  Or were they two independent events?  And what on earth, after 12 years of no issues and very little use would cause the steam unit to blow the cover off the vent? And did I mention this month I forgot to remember pele and rabbit rabbit???", "images": []}

title: Cristallo Blue as Countertop - is bleeding inevitable? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lp2020", "author_name": "Leslie P", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lp2020", "date": "2022-12-20", "text": "We're in the early stages of thinking about a kitchen refresh - the footprint isn't changing;  current plans are to have the cabinets and walls painted, with light hardwood look vinyl planking for the floor, changing out the lighting. Appliances are all stainless now. Have attached a photo of the current place; please excuse the mess and clutter.  BM's Monterey White is the current frontrunner for the cabinets and walls, although we're flexible on the final cream color; only thing is that a sterile white is out.....  The ceiling, however, stays as is :)   Would also plan to replace the current drop-in sink with an undermount workstation sink: https://www.elkay.com/products/details/EFRUAQ31169TWC My problem is with countertops, and concerns I have on bleeding and water absorption. Done lots of reading and research, some great knowledge on this site; and I'm narrowing down the options. We're finding that we're gravitating much more towards natural stone from an aesthetic standpoint, but Marble is not an option (too high maintenance for etching, etc; you can see that this kitchen is used :) ) I'm currently focusing on a crystalline quartzite, Cristallo Blue (This one is labeled as Quarzo Azulado) as one with potential.  Lots of pretty waves and patterns in some of the other quartzites, and some granites too;  but I'm figuring if I can still see the differentiation of grains.... that sand's not fully baked :) Anyway.... I've attached a photo of one quartzite slab we saw recently; official testing still to be done (some bring lemon slices and vinegar; I'm more of the 'HCl 5-10% solution, safety glasses and gloves' type), but I like what I see so far regarding the transformation to a crystal structure, lack of gouges, etc.  And the color variations make for an uncanny match with other design elements in the area of the kitchen.  We're looking at the 3cm thickness for this purpose.  Final selection  would be made once we decide on a fabricator, and go together to inspect what's available.   My question is regarding the findings some have reported with quartzite, and bleeding or moisture wicking into the stone from the edges, particularly close to stoves/sinks.  The sink we're thinking of would require a hole to be cut in the countertop for the faucet, in addition to the the sink itself;  and I'm worried that even with a quartzite as hard as this one is (if the tests bear it out to be a true crystalline quartzite) , that I'm going to be pretty dang mad when i start to see dark edges a few months in..... Another point to keep in mind- typically nightstands are anywhere from 24-30\" wide and 18-36\" deep, so keep that in mind when selecting furniture for this space, especially if you go with a King Size bed and only have 27\" on either side. We would also suggest draperies on the windows to give the room more of a softness and welcoming feel. Hope this feedback is helpful! Side Note: If you are putting a bed on a window wall and it is going to block the window, at least try to make sure the bed is centered on the window, trust us - it will drive you crazy if it is off center when it goes in and it will be very noticeable, because the window is the focal point of the room and the bed amplifies that.", "images": []}}

title: Can I transplant opuntia as double or triple pad (instead of just one) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "otherchuck", "author_name": "otherchuck", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/otherchuck", "date": "2022-12-20", "text": "Greetings, I have been growing cacti for about 40 yrs, so I should know this.  I had some large opuntia \"prickly pear\" cacti fall over recently (in ground, not pot; grew too top heavy compared to root structure) and I cut them up to give to my neighbor to re-home; there are over 60 cuttings.  I know generally people propagate opuntia a single pad at a time, but about half of the cuttings I provided my neighbor with were single pads, while the rest were double or triple pads.  By \"triple,\" for instance, I mean there was the pad that will go in the ground, and there are two pads attached directly to the top of that pad. For \"doubles,\" of course, it is one pad on a pad. I have done the double and triple paradigm in the past, and it seemed to work out fine for me; the advantage is that you of course start with a larger plant.  I don't recall having any trouble with them rooting, even when going directly into native soil (after cut has calloused, of course).  Obviously, for double and triples, the bottom pad would have to go pretty deep in the ground so the weight of any attached pads don't tip it over, but that is doable. But I seem to be the only cactus enthusiast on the planet who does this.  Every single tutorial I have seen online does one pad at a time.  I have to tell my neighbor whether to cut the doubles and triples I gave him into singles, or plant as is, so I am wondering what other people's experiences in this area have been. On the one hand, one might say \"well, if it has worked for you in the past, go for it!\" but at the same time I wonder if maybe I have just gotten lucky or perhaps am blessed with a superior cacti-green-thumb, and I don't want to give my neighbor bad transplanting advice. Thanks for any advice! Otherchuck PS:  Bonus question - How long do you think I should tell my neighbor to let the cut areas on the pads dry out before planting?  If I were doing it myself, I would have a sense for when the cuts looked sufficiently calloused, but I want to give my neighbor a specific time frame.  So far I have told him one week.  Sound about right?  I cut them yesterday and the wounds already looked pretty calloused, so maybe 4 or 5 days?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6232463a03a2375a_5393-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "cactusmcharris", "author_name": "cactusmcharris, interior BC Z4/5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cactusmcharris", "date": "2022-12-21", "text": "oc, You can make a cutting as large as you wish; you just need to support the structure of pads if there are many with a trellis / rocks / other thing to prevent the cutting from falling over. I've done it a number of times; it helps that Opuntias are almost problem-free to root (they are voracious growers, as you no doubt know already, judging from the proliferation of pads in your photo). Callusing for a few days should be enough. If you want to get even more assured of rooting, rooting hormone can be used, though with Opuntias, as implied, it's easy to root with nothing. title: A garden experiment against the coming cold | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "laceyvail", "author_name": "laceyvail 6A, WV", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/laceyvail", "date": "2022-12-21", "text": "For years I've grown savoy cabbages under double row cover and winter lettuce under a little plastic tent set over metal hoops.  It's worked great for years (now that we don't really have much of a winter anymore); last winter I harvested the last cabbage in February.  And today it's a balmy 45 degrees and not even noon yet.  But that's about to change-- tonight starts rain, sleet, wintry mixes through Thursday night with Friday possibly a little snow (unfortunately not enough projected for good insulation) and then Friday night around 0 degrees, Saturday high of 13, Sat night 5. In an effort to save my winter veggies, I just packed hay around and on top of the 5 cabbages and topped that with a double row cover.  When the sun drops below the mountain around 4 this afternoon, I'll lay two tarps over the whole business to keep it all dry.  For the lettuces, I tucked them under a multi layer blanket of row cover and topped that will a lot of hay.  The plastic covering will go back over the hoops when I cover the cabbges. title: Protecting My Citrus From The Hard Freeze | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jdpyn2", "author_name": "John 9a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jdpyn2", "date": "2022-12-22", "text": "I'm in SE Texas and that may be relevant to how best to protect in-ground citrus from a hard freeze. I have heard lots of people repeat instructions they heard that they should cover the roots to protect them from a freeze.  Anyone know where/when that would be helpful?? Here is my setup....a HUGE tarp to cover a mature Satsuma...   View under the tarp:   My goal is to keep the wind out, leave the ground exposed so as to benefit from its relative warmth, and to trap this warmth inside the tarped area. Here is a kumquat in the foreground with a makeshift teepee setup to help support the tarp...and the aforementioned Satsuma in the background.   Done with this part of the yard!  Couple of plum trees in the foreground and a garbage can over the water faucet.   A Ponderosa lemon that has come back nicely from getting frozen back during the 2020 freeze...I'm covering it this time!  It's difficult to get size perspective so, FYI, this one is about 12ft tall.   I wish I could cover some of the other Ponderosa lemons but I ran out of tarps and time so they will have to make it on their own.  Will be interesting to see how the covered one does as compared to the uncovered trees. Good luck to all as this front goes through!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/af92066803a4e72e_1471-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/30321a9203a4e72f_1472-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5272165e03a4e730_1472-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a03233c103a4e731_1473-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fb5227f503a4e731_1474-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "garybeaumont-gw", "author_name": "garybeaumont_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/garybeaumont-gw", "date": "2022-12-23", "text": "I think you did a good job.  I have a couple I did that way except I added mulch around the base of the tree 18 to 24 inches high to try and save the graft.  One lemonade tree was too big to cover, so I added potting soil about 30 inches high around the trunk, again to try and save the graft.  Added the mulch will increase the damage on the exposed areas, but at this point I am only trying to save the graft. title: Fermenting Rose Seeds | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-455777712", "author_name": "Formerly RBEHS Z10A/S17", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-455777712", "date": "2022-12-22", "text": "I've been reading The Art of Fermentation by Sandor Katz--and he mentions that the founders of the Australian Seed Savers' Network recommend fermenting rose seeds for a few days to clean the seeds.  I'm trying this with some Old Master hips, but wonder if anyone has done this or thinks it's necessary to start seedlings.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e4926aa603a4eb14_2474-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "roseseek", "author_name": "roseseek", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roseseek", "date": "2022-12-22", "text": "No, I haven't fermented seeds. I have permitted the hips to rot off rose seeds, which, supposedly inhibits germination according to everything I'd read in old rose books. In my climate, because I can safely, successfully plant rose seeds most of the year without any weather damage (extreme heat, extreme cold, etc.) I just shell and plant or shell and hold them in clean, uncovered baby food jars in the house until I plant them. Can fermenting them to clean them hurt? Probably not. It seems a good experiment to determine if fermenting them will assist in germination. Are you planting a control group of the same seeds to determine whether fermentation affects germination? Supposedly, keeping the seeds damp prior to planting assists germination as it prevents the seed coat from hardening, which would then require a longer period of being damp to allow the two halves to split and the embryo to emerge.", "images": []}}

I usually use experience, time and oven knowledge to cook small cuts of meat, like chops and steaks.  I don't do it often, however, and don't know how to time it for other people and equipment.  So, being that I liked the ONE so much, and Thermoworks has a standard promo that's nearly as good as the specials for just about everything in rotation, I indulged in a ChefAlarm (and got a second to give as a gift). Making a steak for Mr. Picky is easy, usually, but not so much when I'm trying to get food out for everybody else.  I forget it.  And much as I try to tell him to mind it himself, he forgets.  He's good about it--doesn't complain and just eats it, but one does wish to be better.  This time, at our \"big\" small Chanukah dinner, I used the weird oven which I don't know at all, since I had the ChefAlarm, and broiled the steak at 375\u00b0 F on a cast iron grill pan, as usual in the normal oven, but with the probe sticking into the center through the side of the steak. title: Cloths Dryer Exhaust | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hzdeleted-75471404", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-75471404", "date": "2022-12-26", "text": "I am not a professional of any kind having to do with appliances or HVAC. My cloths dryer is an LG electric Model#DLEX3250V I'm pretty sure its 240v. It was installed by the delivery person I think from Sears. The exhaust is a 4inch round port and located on the dryer itself at the bottom basically floor level. The exhaust exits the house through a hole 30\" inches off the floor made through an exterior wall. It has a basic dryer exhaust kit with a one way flap to prevent backflow of air. The dryer is located in my kitchen and the entire length of flexible exhaust duct tube is visible and in the kitchen as well. I think its about 6-8 foot expandable or accordion style flexible hose but the total distance from dryer to wall hole is about 4' ft. I'm guessing. So my question/s or what I've been thinking is whether or not there would be any benefit to making some changes. #1 Move the exit hole to floor level in line with the exit hole from the rear of dryer. #2 Replace flexible accordion style duct tube with the same diameter rigid/solid type duct like you would find on say a woodstove. Or whatever would be most appropriate for cloths dryer duct. Other thought/comment/question: Does the ribbed inside of the flexible exhaust duct slow down airflow and create many pockets where lint eventually can build up which in turn would put more stress and or wear and tear on the machine plus create a fire hazard? I'm sure this style of exhaust tube makes installation much easier but I would think that one benefit alone would not make up for all the drawbacks. Wouldn't solid or rigid tubing with a smooth bore be the longest lasting, most efficient option and also need the least amount of maintenance/replacement despite it not being the easiest to install? Or am I totally overthinking this whole thing HaHa Thanks in advance for any responses and thanks for reading!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "user-pfvwus-pf~726048410", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/general-contractors/user-pfvwus-pf~726048410", "date": "2022-12-26", "text": "Rigid ducting is code because of the high fire risk associated with flex duct.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2022-12-26", "text": "A clothes dryer duct can be flexible for the transition piece. That is the portion between the dryer and the permanent duct connection at the wall. It must remain exposed and less than 8' long. It is code allowed. The portion in or through the wall, however, must be solid and smooth. The kinds of ducts for the transition piece are as follows:   1. plastic flex which is the worst 2. rigid, don't use the aluminum thinwall duct in the dryer section of the big box store, move an aisle over to the sheetmetal in the HVAC section and pick the 25ga, 26ga, or 30ga duct whichever they carry on hand 3. foil flex which is also crapola 4. semi-rigid aluminum flex is the one if you choose flex If you plan to lower the vent wall cap, that means you'll have to patch the inside and outside walls, not to mention cutting a clean 4 1/8\" dia hole. title: Frost protection | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hzdeleted-25649216", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-25649216", "date": "2022-12-26", "text": "I'm looking for peoples experiences with frost protection for shrubs and other perenials. I'm in zone 9, but we have been having these freezes that drop the temps into teens or low 20s for a couple of nights once or twice in the winter. The rest of the time it could be 60-40F. I've been using frost blankets and sometimes xmas lights+ frost blankets with varying results.  My gardenias with just frost blankets have brown leaves, but the plants made it overall. Roses with no cover are 70% damaged, with cover 30% damaged, with double cover - no damage at all. Surprisingly my Autumn Azaleas have a destroyed foliage and blooms after using the blankets. I was under impression that they are pretty freeze hardy. Tropical hibiscus and mandevilla survived outside under a blanket with only leaf damage. Poet's jasmine has split bark in a couple spots, also was covered. My neighbor's hawthorns that leaf-burned to a brown crisp last freeze, and took 6 months to come back, have no damage this time around without any special intervention. A few thoughts that are tumbling around in my head - do frost blankets freeze-burn leaves where they touch? The results seem to be mixed based on my experience. Is it possible to \"freeze train\" your plants to survive and stay evergreen? Would doubling up on frost blankets be better? Thank you so much!", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "oberon476", "author_name": "oberon476", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oberon476", "date": "2022-12-28", "text": "@grad_girl_1, do you have multiple windows like that, or is it just one window? If it's one window, what room is it in? \" Broken glass panes, lost seals can allow cold, outside air to penetrate inside plus let warm air escape...\"  from the link....As I read this, I see it as referring to window seal not glass seal, but it's hard to say for sure. In any case, a lost IG seal will not result in what you are seeing, while a lost window seal might. IG or dual pane glass packages are sealed for three reasons. In no particular order of priority, first to protect LowE coating, second to allow for gas (usually argon) fill, and third to allow the use of sufficient desiccant in the airspace to keep the space dry which lowers the dew point inside the space to a level that whatever tiny amount of moisture remains in the space will not condensate inside the space. Losing the seal does three things. First the argon gas will escape, second ambient air will enter the space resulting in corrosion of the LowE coating, and third because the desiccant becomes saturated, the dew point within the space will rise to a level where condensation can (and will) form inside the space. Worst case, a seal failure might raise the IG U factor by .05 or so, it will not result in the sort of surface condensation/ice that you are seeing. Whether or not you have a LowE coating, what spacer is used in the IG construction, and the material and design of the window frame will all affect the formation of condensation much more than will an IG seal failure, but why your glass is below freezing is the primary question, and IG seal failure would not cause that. There could be a problem in the seal between the glass and the sash or a weatherseal issue allowing cold outside air to penetrate that seal and cooling the inside glass way down. I would be very surprised if assuming that you warmed the glass enough to melt the ice and dry the glass, then removed the screen and left any curtains open and you still experienced ice formation like that, unless that window was in a bathroom which would explain moisture but not  that much ice. title: Floof! Rate your year! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "amylou321", "author_name": "amylou321", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/amylou321", "date": "2022-12-28", "text": "On a scale of 1-10 rate how 2022 treated you and why! Me, I give it a solid 7/10. On the one hand, its been okay. I still have a good job and a happy home life with SO. No health problems, car problems, major house problems, etc. And that is satisfactory enough. On the other hand, 2022 lost points because this year: I lost 2 of my dogs, and it was devastating. One, was not a huge surprise. He was 10, which is pretty old for such a big dog. I noticed he was having a hard time getting around and the vet recommended aspirin for him, which helped for a few months. Then, I saw it. I lump. A hard lump forming on his backside. I knew then it was over. The other one, that was a shock and horrible. After Otis died, Buster stopped eating. I thought he was just sad, they were best friends. After a week, I took him to the vet because he had begun to lose weight. The vet, after blood work and an xray, said give him time and in the meantime gave him steroids. After another week, I took him to a different vet who, after more blood tests and an xray, also attributed his lethargy, refusal to eat and weight loss as grief and told me to give him people food in the meantime to entice him to eat. SO called me at work one night to tell me he was gone. It was a VERY hot day, so the dogs were inside. He went to let them out once the sun went down and it was cooler outside and Buster would not get up from his bed. HE was gone. He was only 6 years old and I am still upset that 2 vets and hundreds of dollars worth of tests could not help him. I do not in any way believe it was grief that took him so quickly. Something was wrong. I am still mad about it months later. I still have 3 dogs and George the cat, so I try to count my blessings. But GRRRRRRRRR. I also lost people this year. My aunt underwent a Bone marrow transplant to combat her cancer, only for an unidentified infection that was allowed to become out of control to end her life. It was really sad, because she has been fighting tooth and nail against her cancer. It was heartbreaking to see her finally realize she had lost and accept it. And a coworker of mine took his own life, shocking EVERYONE that knew him. It hit me a lot harder than I would expect it to. Everyone was in tears when we heard the news. And if he took that step because of the reason his wife SAID he did, it was infuriating, because it was something that could have been overcome. So it was a miserable mix of grief and anger that took hold of me for longer than it should have. He was such a kind man, and always so much fun to work with when I had the opportunity. My sister was diagnosed with cancer this year at age 39. And though her prognosis seems good, it is hard to watch her suffer from afar and not be able to do anything. It was traumatizing for her to have to shave her head, and I can relate to that. She told me it was more traumatizing than her mastectomy. And while she has a great attitude overall, her diagnosis at such an early age has doomed me to worry about her for the rest of our lives. I will NEVER believe that she is cancer free. And I will NEVER believe that her doctors are doing enough to keep her healthy. And I am angry that this has happened to her.  Hopefully next year will see better health for her. My father had a pretty scary health incident. He went from a perfectly healthy and active man to not being able to walk without help VERY quickly. He suffered with a sudden burst intestine and it was very lucky they were able to identify and fix it in time. His recovery had been slow and while I and my other sister have been doing what we can to help our mom, it is very much a drain on her, even with the professional help she is getting. My father is not abusive, but he is stubborn and demanding and is one of those men that thinks he knows better than everyone, including his doctors. I can see my mother having to talk herself out of whacking him one good time when he has one of his little fits, the saint. Work has been fine. I got a decent raise and a nice bonus. I also got into a NASTY tiff with HR a few months ago, regarding some of THEIR practices that they refuse to admit fault in. And it is always a bad feeling when you realize you cannot win, even when you are 100 RIGHT. I am still salty about it. The snakes. Also, in my department we have had a bit of a shake up. One person quit, another announced his retirement, and therefore of course, 2 new people were hired, which can be stressful with all the overtime and new dynamics. One of the new hires is the wife of someone who works there in another department. She is really nice, quite funny, learned quickly, is well liked by the drivers and people in other departments we work with (and us), and generally fit in really well. She is lovely and everyone breathed a sigh of relief that FINALLY, everyone gets along!!!! She is a bit high strung and tends to get stressed over minor things, but that will improve with time I think. The other, is the son of someone else that works there. His mother has been there over 40 years. And he is, well, nothing like the first one I mentioned. BUT, my boss hired him and he is HIS problem now, as he refused to listen to all of our input regarding his horrible performance and nasty, arrogant and entitled attitude. And his habit of taking meetings and conference calls for his other job (life insurance salesman) instead of paying attention when we are trying to train him. And his need to go visit his mommy in her office everyday for an hour or more. We do not GET lunch breaks or any other set break times. We have to be in or at least around or office at all times in case a truck comes in or someone calls needing help. I have NO idea why he is allowed to carry on like that. But, like I said, not my problem and while I am stressed about it because I want everyone to get along and work together well, i accept that it is out of my hands and will mind my own business. It is unfortunate for him that he will be turned loose on his own next week, when the other night minion officially retires. He still, after 2 months of us trying to train him, does not know basic things because he is more worried about looking at his phone and selling life insurance than he was trying to learn his new duties there. Lucky for him though, the first new hire I mentioned requested to be moved to night shift, so he will be on days and will have my boss to help him some of the time. I can only hope that everything works out, no matter what that looks like. All that being whined about, I am determined to count my blessings and acknowledge my overall happiness and good quality of life. And I am determined to face next year with optimism that ALL will get better. Bring it on 2023. I. Am. Ready.", "images": []}

title: Follow up on the "year of experiences & activities" gift | Houzz Forum

She said that it was really the very best gift she's ever received and that she couldn't stop smiling the next day. Most importantly, I have seen that she's been much lighter and happier. I scaled it back quite a bit and kept the activities local because ... 1. I didn't want to plan things that she may not be up to physically. 2. The Grandkids really showed up and had some great plans so I didn't want to overwhelm with 100s of activities/invites. Some activities included gifts... some included gift cards. Some activities were things for her to do on her own (try a new recipe, snuggle in and watch Outlander, get a chair massage and pedicure)... and others are with one family member or a group (take her daughters to brunch at a cool new place in our hometown, go to an herb shoppe). I included things that she would need to plan and coordinate ... a bubble party with the great grandsons with a suggestion to make cake pops ... make a lunch date with a friend from the old neighborhood .... a poolside brunch with the family where she would plan the meal but we'd help prepare. The grandkids came up with some great ideas too-- I think it made the gift so much more rich and meaningful. They contributed ideas like teaching one how to make crab cakes, watching a Phillies game (with a gift bag of cracker jack, hot dogs and beer), an invitation for a homemade italian dinner, a trip to a local winery). It was truly a group effort! I provided most of the gifts and gift cards but the ideas came from all! I also took Localeater's idea to create a family calendar to keep track of the activities and events-- and to add to it. I told mom this is a starting point... she should come up with the things she wants to do too! I could have done better with more time and more planning but I was very pleased with how it turned out. Ich durfte mal einen Bungalow betreten, der zwischen der \"\u00f6ffentlichen Zone\" und der \"Privaten Zone\" des Hauses einen kleinen \"Durchgang\" hatte, der sich wie eine kleine Raumblase weitete und dort einen kleinen feinen Medienbereich ergab. Sie schreiben ja selbst: ein kleiner Runder Tisch, wo man sich zu zweit nicht verloren f\u00fchlt, und ein 12-Personen-Tisch, wenn mal wieder alle gleichzeitig da sind, das w\u00e4re toll. Sonst w\u00e4re es ja kein empirisches Hindernis nur den gro\u00dfen Tisch zu nehmen, auch wenn man allein daran sitzt. Jeder Bereich in Ihrem Zuhause hat eine ganz eigene Aufgabe, der er gerecht werden sollte. Ein lebendiger Essbereich f\u00fcr die ganze Familie ist da ganz anders als der Wohnraum-Bereich, der eher leiser ist und wo die Gespr\u00e4che innerhalb der Sitzenden bleiben, ist wieder ganz anders als die K\u00fcche, in der konzentriert gearbeitet oder mit mehreren auch gelacht wird, und ab und an rennt jemand mit den Abf\u00e4llen raus. Ebenso ist ein Schlafplatz etwas anderes als die Privatboutique, als der Medien-R\u00fcckzugsraum, und das Bad zum Schlafraum sollte auch klar zum Schlafraum geh\u00f6ren und nicht erst durch mehrere \"laute\" Bereiche erreichbar sein. Er sollte eine klare Einladung sein, ein Opening f\u00fcr alles, was noch kommt, und nat\u00fcrlich auch eine Schnittstelle zwischen Innen und Au\u00dfen, die genug Platz bietet, sich auf das Ankommen oder Losgehen vorzubereiten, durch Garderobenplatz, vllt. ein WC, eine Sitzgelegenheit und Schl\u00fcsselablage und genug Platz f\u00fcr Schuhe der G\u00e4ste. Den G\u00e4sten vorbehaltene Platz sollte aber nicht die gesamte Woche \u00fcber zeigen, da\u00df keiner da ist und das Haus doch viel zu leer und gro\u00df ist. Mir fallen da spontan mindestens 5 verschiedene M\u00f6glichkeiten an, so da\u00df ich nicht zu eng um nur eine L\u00f6sung herum versuchen w\u00fcrde, das zu planen. All das, was ich bis hierhin angesprochen habe hat gar nichts mit dem ziehen von W\u00e4nden zu tun, sondern mit der Frage, wie Sie wohnen. Und in erster Linie leben wir gl\u00fccklicherweise alle in der Zeit und erleben nicht alles gleichzeitig. Ebenso sollten wir auch unsere R\u00e4ume gestalten, da\u00df wir nicht sagen, da\u00df ein Raum alles, und erst recht nicht alles glecihzeitig erf\u00fcllen k\u00f6nnen muss, besonders nicht unvereinbare Aufgaben (zB. Ruhe vs. Laut). Ja, es gibt \"Geschmack\" und leider auch viel mehr Meinung als Wissen, aber wenn es um Wohnen geht, geht es in erster Linie um den Menschen und seine Lebensgewohnheiten darin. Und das ist eine Konstante mit bestimmten gesetztm\u00e4\u00dfigkeiten. Alles abweichende ist einfach nur experiment und \"fehl am Platz\". Es hat seinen Grund, da\u00df Ihnen die \"klaren und strukturierten\" Entw\u00fcrfe von Frau Redecker gefallen, und es hat seine Gr\u00fcnde, warum sich dieses \"oh ja!\" Gef\u00fchl in Ihrem letzten Entwurf, auch wenn er doch scheinbar alles enth\u00e4lt, was Sie wollen, einfach nicht einstellen will. Es sind viele Gedanken eingeflossen, aber kein Gedanke an den Menschen und wie er darin wohnt. Ein Sprichwort sagt \"das erste Haus bauen wir f\u00fcr unsere Feine, das zweite f\u00fcr Freunde, und das dritte f\u00fcr uns selbst\". Das hat ganz klar damit zu tun, da\u00df wir zunehmend die \"will haben\" gegen \"so will ich leben\" eintauschen, weil wir uns zunehmend durch das Leben in den drei Stadien der Entw\u00fcrde kennenlernen. Auch etwas, was mit Zeit zu tun hat. Jeder Link zu Grundrissen, die Sie lieben werden, wird dennoch nicht zu Ihnen oder dem Grundst\u00fcck passen, Daher fragte ich vor einem Jahr noch, welcher Lebens-Stil es vllt. werden darf. \"Der eher Nordische\" schreiben Sie da, und jetzt pr\u00e4sentieren Sie ein Geb\u00e4ude, da alles, nur nicht die nordische Architektur widerspiegelt. Innen und Au\u00dfen bedingen sich ganz klar. Ich kann nicht in den ersten Gedanken nur das Innere betrachten, und das \u00c4u\u00dfere einfach folgen lassen. Allein die Ramh\u00f6he ist eklatant entscheidend. Und je nach Raumgr\u00f6\u00dfe hat ein und dieselbe Raumh\u00f6he eine v\u00f6llig andere Wirkung, weshalb es eben doch eine Rolle spielt, da\u00df nicht ganz kleine R\u00e4ume neben ganz gro\u00dfen liegen, ohne die Wirkung dazu zu betrachten. Wir alle haben mal lange Zeiten investiert, um \"den richtigen Menschen\" zu finden. Freunde, Zahnarzt, Bankberater, Lieblingsrestaurant, Hausarzt, Florist, B\u00e4ckerei der Lieblingskuchen,... Niemand sagt, es wird mit der Suche nach Planern leichter. Es braucht jemanden, der Ihnen die richtigen Fragen stellt, und sich aufgrund seines Wissens auch mal \u00fcber Ihr \"das muss so!\" schweigend hinwegsetzt, um Ihnen aufzuzeigen, da\u00df Sie das richtige wollten, Ihre Vorstellung der Umsetzung nur nicht passt. Fast jeder gro\u00dfartige Entwurf beginnt mit einer einfachen Skizze auf einem St\u00fcck Papier. Da wird das Grundst\u00fcck hingekritzelt, die Licht und die Windrichtung in gro\u00dfen Linien wie ein Gedanke zu Papier gebracht, und einzelne Kreise in unterschiedlichen Gr\u00f6\u00dfen definieren die einzelnen Bereiche die wichtig / notwendige sind. Zwischen den Kreisen und um sie herum sind deren Beziehungen durch Linien und Pfeile angedeutet. Und je gr\u00f6\u00dfer eine Fl\u00e4che wird, umso wichtiger ist es, da\u00df die einzelnen Bereiche untereinander kleine Einheiten bilden und diese wiederum sich zu gr\u00f6\u00dferen verketten. Daraus entstehen Bewegungsmuster und Verbindungszentren. Und erst dann wird konkretisiert. Genau das ist der Grund, warum hier niemand eine Skizze bieten kann und erst recht nicht an einem Bestand etwas ver\u00e4ndern kann, ohne gleich alle Zusammenh\u00e4nge zu zerst\u00f6ren. title: How to eliminate Whiteflies on Indoor Hibiscus | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "doriswk", "author_name": "doriswk", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/doriswk", "date": "2022-12-28", "text": "I have 2 hibiscus plants that are ca 20 - 25 years old. During each summer I keep them outdoors, and treat them with insecticidal soap and neem oil plus a bit of E.O. of peppermint several times before and after bringing them indoors. This year I sprayed them already 3 times before returning indoors, including three very small new hibiscus plants, yet the whitefly infestation is worse than any other year.  Typically I cut the plants back late fall so there are not many leaves to spray. But this year a hurricane had severely damaged the leaves so  I cut the plants back in June which disrupted the usual outdoor flowering period. They did not start blooming till September and are covered in blooms now, see pics.  I Really  want to enjoy the blooms a bit longer, but am getting super tired of spraying these plants while having the adult flies lift off and temporarily park themselves someplace else. I bet they are watching me mopping up the big soapy puddles from the kitchen floor. It does not take them long to return to the hibiscus plants. I have started to spray my Christmas cacti as well, as I can  see the odd white fleck on them too. Aside from  giving the two large plants a severe \"haircut\" , is there anything else I can eliminate the whiteflies with?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3362dbb303ac9b0e_6387-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2022-12-29", "text": "I would use some yellow sticky traps to remove/eliminate the adult white flies. White flies can rapidly develop a resistance to any common and frequently applied insecticidal sprays, so at the very least, rotate your products. If you can move your plant(s) into the shower and wash them down well, especially the leaf undersides, that could help a lot. I would also consider using neem oil as a soil drench and in that way it will act as a systemic so less concern about using a contact spray and missing many flies :-) And getting it all over the house. btw, those are two very handsome plants, white flies or not!!", "images": []}}

title: Is this P.V.C drain legal according to plumbing code? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "service1956", "author_name": "service1956", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/service1956", "date": "2022-12-28", "text": "My wife and I had a new house built. We love it. But, we had a problem. The night before Christmas my wife came to me and said that the toilet would not flush. Used a plunger for about 30 minutes with no results. So I went to the basement to look at the drain plumbing for that toilet. I also found that the two sinks in the same bathroom would not drain. So I knew the flow was not blocked inside the toilet. So I took a picture of where I thought the blockage was.   The 90 degree bend on the left dropping down is for the toilet. The middle 45 degree bend is for the two sinks that would not drain. I could hear a faint trickle inside the pipe in the area of the second 90 degree bend on the right. So I figured that was where the blockage was. After about almost an hour, I went back up and flushed the toilet. Got lucky!! The blockage cleared itself and had no problem sense then. My question is this: Is that 90 degree elbow on the right legal according to code? I'm thinking there should have been two 45s installed to cut down that sharp bend. White Chicken Chili INGREDIENTS: \u00a8 1 sweet medium onion, diced \u00a8 1/2 cup butter or Smart Balance \u00a8 1/2 cup flour \u00a8 2 1/2 cups chicken broth \u00a8 1 1/2 teaspoons chile powder \u00a8 1 teaspoon cumin \u00a8 1/2 teaspoon salt \u00a8 1/2 teaspoon white pepper \u00a8 40 ounces Great Northern Beans, rinsed (Bush\u2019s cans are 15.8 oz each) \u00a8 2 small cans (4oz) chopped green chiles, undrained \u00a8 White rotisserie chicken meat, shredded (approx. 2 cups) \u00a8 2 cups plain, full-fat Greek yogurt (or sour cream) \u00a8 2 cups shredded Monterey Jack cheese \u00a8 Garnish, if desired, with any or all: diced avocado, cilantro, a dollop of more yogurt, sliced jalapenos DIRECTIONS: 1) Add chopped onion and butter to a large soup pot and saut\u00e9 on medium for a few minutes. 2) In a medium measuring cup or bowl, first add the 1/2 cup of flour. We met with our client to work out how they live in the house, what spaces we had to work with and how we can adapt the rooms, so they function well, all while looking stylish, particularly the front room.   Very quickly we learnt that the dining room had never been used to dine at and that our clients had no intention of retaining it as a dining space. There was an under used spare room upstairs that could function as a home office and still have room for a sofa bed when needed as the occasional guest room, so it was easy to move the workstation upstairs. We also learnt that while yoga is a great passion, stretching into the downward dog beside the front door was not ideal.   Upstairs on the landing area we found an under used living room with a sofa that was over sized for the space and made the area difficult to use. We decided to replace the existing sofa with a much smaller sofa that was more inviting for the room and also left plenty of room for yoga at home and out of site from the front door! To the front room, our clients wanted a beautiful living area and a space that has a sense of arrival from the front door. title: When neighbors become family….. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rhizo-1", "author_name": "rhizo_1 (North AL) zone 7", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rhizo-1", "date": "2022-12-30", "text": "Many of you know the story of the Sprites and their caregiver grandfather, our neighbor.  Several years ago, these two little girls wheedled their way into our lives and hearts\u2026..long story, but we are now a community of five, with all of the legal rights required to raise two girls. Our across the street neighbors, a young professional couple, have become good friends\u2026.we help each other out.  He took my husband to the surgery center recently, stayed with him, and brought him home to me, just for example.  Her mother comes to stay with their blind and deaf dog whenever they have to go out of town and we sort of keep an eyeball on the mother when she\u2019s here.  Not that she needs it but appreciates that we are watching out for her. Another much loved neighbor has recently contracted kidney cancer.  Her adult children are near and are a huge support,  and we add our support to theirs. Healthful foods, good company,  joy rides to the country, a bit of wine over our backyard fire.   In the past, her son took over our lawn care when my husband had his hip replacement.  He came to my husband for comfort when his Dad died. Our other next door neighbor, a young bachelor, was jilted by his fiancee not long ago and was grief stricken.  The Sprites were heartbroken for him and smothered him with cookies and pies and handdrawn artwork, until he was all smiles again.  I expect that there was some bad mouthing of the ex involved when they went to visit. All of this came to mind when the recipe of the white chicken chile was posted.  My very first thought was that it would be a welcomed treat for these family members, my neighbors.", "images": []}

I had them \u2019trained\u2019 to stay out of our yard unless invited so they would stand with their toes on an imaginary property line until I would relent. title: On the same note as Rhizo's post | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jasdip1", "author_name": "Jasdip", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jasdip1", "date": "2022-12-30", "text": "This was in our paper and it brought tears of joy to my eyes. Being a Good Samaritan, and a good neighbour is absolutely priceless. I was telling someone about this a couple of days ago, and I got choked up telling it. I travelled this highway daily when I lived in Listowel, and it can be brutal! WALLENSTEIN \u2014 The snow is piling up, burying the car deeper and deeper into the snowbank. Deb Dooling-Westover pulls out her crackers, cream cheese and roasted red pepper jelly, and offers some to her husband, Mark Westover. In the back seat, a hitchhiker takes a few for himself. He\u2019s on his way to Listowel for his daughter\u2019s first Christmas with a bag full of toys and a few pairs of spare clothes, but his taxi has long ago turned around and left him on Line 86, just outside of Wallenstein. The back seat of the Westovers\u2019 car is his only chance at warmth for the night. The car\u2019s not moving; the snow drift had made sure of that, and the trio are settling in for a long, cold night. Snowplows can\u2019t get to them, and there\u2019s no way in or out of the country road. The Westovers \u2014 Deb, 63, and Mark, 71 \u2014 and their hitchhiker, a young man of about 30, are trapped. They\u2019re talking, but their eyes dart nervously at the fuel gauge that\u2019s slowly ticking lower. The snow is filling up the windows, and they\u2019re equally worried that a car might come piling in behind them. It\u2019s Christmas Eve, and a winter storm bringing heavy snow and wind gusts of 100 km/h has shut down much of the province on one of the busiest travel days of the year. On this rural road, 30 kilometres north of Kitchener, it feels as if nothing and nobody is around you. It\u2019s a vast rural area, dotted with Mennonite farms and sprawling fields. The Westovers are on their way from Ayr to spend Christmas with friends in Wingham. They spent the morning checking the weather to make sure the roads were still open when they left just before noon. The further they drive, the worse the conditions get. Eventually, on a long stretch of farmland between Wallenstein and Macton, there is no going any further. There are a few other cars stuck in the area. As the winds pick up and blow the snow in blankets across the farm fields and over the road, it gets harder to make them out. Each car is an island, and the snow is gobbling them up. After a few hours sitting inside the car, Deb looks out of the snow-covered window and rubs her eyes to make sure she\u2019s not hallucinating. A man with a pair of snowshoes has emerged from the snowbank. He knocks on the side of the car, and she opens it up. \u201cDo you have food and water?\u201d he asks. \u201cWell, we don\u2019t have a lot of food, but we have some water and Diet Coke in our cooler,\u201d she tells him. \u201cMy car is behind my husband\u2019s; I only have a quarter tank of gas.\u201d The Westovers had filled their two cars with presents, and they were hoping to do some work on Deb\u2019s fuel tank once they got to their friend\u2019s house. She had been following Mark the whole drive, but both of their cars were now stuck in the snowdrift. \u201cDon\u2019t worry,\u201d he says. \u201cI have lots of gas. I\u2019ll come back for you later.\u201d An hour goes by. It\u2019s dark now. With the wind chill, it feels like -27C. The snow continues to fall and the wind is howling. A roar starts up behind them, and Deb jumps out of the car to see approaching blue and red lights. Their man in the snowshoes has returned, this time in a tractor. He gets Deb back into her car, pulls it out, and then pulls out Mark and the hitchhiker. By this point, the tractor has already pulled out some of the other cars as well. Once they\u2019re safely back on the road, he asks the occupants of all the cars \u2014 about six in total \u2014 to follow him about a kilometre down the road and into a long driveway, where they come to a stop at a farmhouse. The group walks into the house to find the man\u2019s wife peeling carrots in the kitchen, with two young boys bouncing around the house. They are a modern Mennonite family, and the farmhouse is equipped with power, heating and a family phone. \u201cI\u2019ve never spent any time with a Mennonite family or been inside a (Mennonite) house before,\u201d Deb said later. \u201cAnd I have to tell you, these were the most beautiful people I\u2019ve ever met.\u201d Deb joins the woman in the kitchen, helping to peel carrots. Then she watches as she puts potatoes through a food processor, throws them into a boiling pot, strains them, and mixes them with some cream and butter to make mashed potatoes. Then she starts cooking summer sausage as more people start piling in to the farmhouse \u2014 there\u2019s about a dozen of them now.  The family has some table extensions, and by the time dinner is served, it\u2019s a feast for nearly 16 people, each with a spot around the \u201charvest table.\u201d They say a silent prayer, and the dinner begins. \u201cI was literally crying,\u201d said Deb. \u201cIt was the most unbelievable thing I had ever seen in my life. There we were, thinking we were going to freeze to death. We really thought we were going to die. And now we\u2019re all seated around this table, warm, and having dinner at this farmhouse.\u201d Around the table, the different groups recount their stories. Each talk about watching the weather advisories, checking to make sure the roads were open, and eventually finding themselves stuck in the snow drift with no way out. But something still doesn\u2019t quite add up. How did this man know to come looking for them? One of the women at the table speaks up. While she was waiting in her car, she had noticed a name on a mailbox. She called her son in Listowel, and he started calling all the numbers in the area with the same last name. Eventually, he got through to the man, who threw on his snowshoes, and headed out into the storm to see if he could find them. Not wanting any unnecessary attention, the family has asked to keep their names private. \u201cI don\u2019t want any honour or glory,\u201d the man told the Record. \u201cIt\u2019s the Lord\u2019s glory, and we did our Christian duty.\u201d After dinner is over, the family eventually leads Deb and Mark to a spare bedroom to hunker down for the night. It is cold in the room, but the blankets keep them warm. The rest of the travellers are spread out around the house, sleeping on makeshift beds and couches. In the morning, Deb runs to the car to grab some peameal bacon she had planned to cook on Christmas morning. Many of the others do the same, bringing in what spare food they can contribute to the feast. Like the night before, they cook up a big meal, each sitting around the table to enjoy a Christmas breakfast. When the food is finished, they clean up together, and then start piling back into their cars, each bound to family and friends. None of them know each other. After they say their goodbyes and wish each other luck for the journeys ahead, all they\u2019re left with is a handful of first names and memories of faces, warmth and a reminder of the good in people when tragedy strikes. The Westovers \u201cwere so careful, and they spent the whole day making sure the roads were open,\u201d said Brenda Szasz, the friend in Wingham that the Westovers were travelling to visit. \u201cThey did their final check and let us know they were coming. I guess they were in for quite the adventure.\u201d Deb and Mark do eventually reach their final destination. The gifts they had piled into their cars make it to the friends and family they planned to see. And as they sit around the table for Christmas dinner, they tell the story of a snowy country road, and the man on the snowshoes who appeared out of nowhere, and took them to safety in a farmhouse with his family.  \u201cI have to tell you, it was the most beautiful Christmas ever,\u201d said Deb.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "sstrawn9", "author_name": "susan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sstrawn9", "date": "2022-12-30", "text": "I have LG minisplits, a multi-head system with 4 heads. Before I fix all the drywall and floor damage, I'd like to see whether anyone has a solution?  the only suggestion I've received is to pour clorox or vinegar down the drain every month.  This sounds easier than it is, since one requires a full ladder to reach, and taking the cover off isn't easy.  Not really the maintenance I thought I was buying in to. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~312471206", "author_name": "Austin Air Companie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~312471206", "date": "2023-01-02", "text": "This sounds easier than it is, since one requires a full ladder to reach, and taking the cover off isn't easy. Not really the maintenance I thought I was buying in to. I know (now) that leaking is a well-known problem with these systems, but I really don't know how they can continue to be sold when they cause so much damage, completely unpredictably and without warning. Is there something in particular that would be helpful? Susan, Yeah unfortunately that's the way it goes for mini splits, the other is if you start some sort clorox or vinegar treatment this may lead to other issues that tend to be more costly, not that those things won't eventually happen anyway, but these sorts of treatments tend to speed these wear issues up. (freon leaks) Most mini split models will drain via a gravity drain on an exterior wall of the structure. I would say it's important this drain is as short as possible has no loops or traps in it (mini split exterior drained unit only) AND a completely vertical drain or as vertical as possible. The idea is that when the system runs the condensate evacuates the entirety of the condensate drain. It will likely clog again, the idea is to minimize it. If for some reason the mini split head (indoor unit) was not placed on an exterior wall, your maintenance troubles will be harder to rectify. If water is allowed to sit in a horizontal drain run, it will start growth and or tiny dust particles that eventually fill the drain tube. Size of the drain tube (diameter) for these kinds of appliances are often times quite small so they are \"designed\" more or less to have these kinds of problems. The manufacturers cover their bases well within the confines of these arguments to include: We're not responsible for maintenance. Typically the mini splits are hung on an exterior wall the line set runs down that wall and to the exterior condensing unit. Some condenser models may have the ability to feed multiple heads (the indoor boxes that hang on the wall) while others may have a  condensing unit for each head. Each head will (should) have it's own separate gravity fed condensate tube (drain tube). Some models like cassettes that fit in ceiling space will come with condensate pumps that will pump the water out of the condensate reservoir these may also include some shut off device if the pump ever fails. Take a picture of the line set arrangement outside and you should be able to see where these condensate drains terminate (drain to). This may also give a few hints as to why you're having trouble so frequently.", "images": []}}

title: garlic is a LOT more cold tolerant than onion | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2022-12-30", "text": "I have several rows of onions and garlic. I put them in in November and they were about 8 inches high.  We had a HIGHLY unusual freeze last week, where the temperature went down to 10F (shades of the HIGHLY unusual freeze we had here two years ago!). I figured they needed some protection, so I covered the onions but neglected to cover the garlic. Guess what. The onions were flattened, and all leaves were killed. The crop is saved though, as the root bulbs survived, and new shoots are coming out of all of them. But the garlic was virtually untouched. All the green in them remains, and while they were a bit bent and droopy, they are now pretty vertical and look entirely happy. I'm slightly stunned. They're all alliums. I know that both are cold-tolerant, but I've never seen their cold tolerance compared like this.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "george-welsh80", "author_name": "George Welsh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/george-welsh80", "date": "2022-12-30", "text": "I haven't changed anything except moving the plant to a draughty cold room (didn't think it would drop as low as -5 in London). other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "george-welsh80", "author_name": "George Welsh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/george-welsh80", "date": "2022-12-30", "text": "", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e142ae6003af6e35_1402-w240-h320-b0-p0--.jpg"]}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "ken-adrian", "author_name": "ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ken-adrian", "date": "2022-12-31", "text": "how long ago was the cold event?? i think it is cold damage ... lets see other plants in the room with damage from the same event to compare ... the length of time it takes.. to show the damage.. is usually indicative of how severe the damage is.. meaning.. if its showing in a few days.. its pretty bad ... many .. if not most plants.. with no insult to the root mass ... presuming the pot didnt freeze .. can easily recover form cold events... but with very slow growing plants.. it will seem to take forever.. and might be worthwhile to just get rid of a common injured plant.. just so it doesnt bum you out every day looking at it ...it would be worth a couple pounds just to get it out of mind ... ken", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "rina-", "author_name": "rina_Ontario,Canada 5a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rina-", "date": "2022-12-31", "text": "-5 C ia pretty cold. It would be even worse if plant was wet (potting medium...) It also depends on how long & what is the lowest temp for the plant. Google min temps for any plant you have been wondering about.  If frost damage, hope the stem is not affected. I would be happier if tips were damaged...they would just dry up. BUT it is difficult to know from the photo.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "mark-sammons16", "author_name": "Marco", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mark-sammons16", "date": "2023-01-01", "text": "I'm no expert, just an amateur who grows several kinds of these South African plants. Your appears to be either Aloe ferox or Aloe merlothii. In my garden here in the Sonoran Desert that straddles the US/Mexican border, my several aloes are planted in the ground, so I don't have the option of moving them indoors when temperatures drop below freezing. (Yes, we do get frosts several times each winter; and routine June days of 110). If winter dawn temperatures drop below 29 F (about -1.6 C), I cover my aloes with cloths raised on stakes so the fabric doesn't touch the leaves. As with all succulents, if the plant is too plumped with water when frost comes, the plant is more vulnerable to damage as cells freeze and rupture. I water mine with a frequency based on temperatures, viz.:  90+ weekly; 80s alternate weeks; 70s every three weeks; 60 or below monthly or less. These tidy and easy-to-remember Farenheit numbers translate to Celcius at about 32.2+ weekly; 26.6+  alternate weeks; 21+ every three weeks; 15.5 monthly or less. If in doubt -- as when temperatures are variable, or there has been a lot of rain -- skip watering for a week. Getting to your question: I think the small grey ovoid thumb-print-sized spots are likely frost damage, which may turn blackish as they rot. Be very restrained with watering, to minimize expansion of rot spots. The bands of irregular green will probably even out. The tannish band across the base of that one leaf looks like it is preparing to die. Let it become brittle and rigid enough to snap off. From time to time, bend it gently; if it does not snap, leave it alone. If it will not snap off, do not cut if off, as that would expose living interior flesh to bacteria that will promote rot. Keep an eye on the spots; if they stay the same size, even if they blacken, the rest of the leaf should be okay. Eventually the leaf will age out as new ones grow out from the center, and when the old leaf becomes russet and brittle you can snap it off. In your photo, the soil looks both heavy and wet, and the pot plastic. If you can find a sack of cactus soil, re-pot the aloe in an unglazed terracotta pot, and raise the pot on clay feet or a bed of pebbles. Raising the pot allows the soil to drain rapidly when you water it, and the terracotta pot allows the soil to breath. These two types of aloe grow in the African wild in open grasslands, which is to say they can take as much sun as you can give them (other aloes prefer bright dappled shade). As another writer has suggested, you can always start with a new plant. If you pursue that, wait till weather warms a bit, and start out with the right soil and pot and watering schedule. Good luck with this, as everyone benefits from a bit of green in their lives. main_question: {"author_id": "karptonite", "author_name": "Daniel", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/karptonite", "date": "2022-12-31", "text": "I posted an an earlier question on this same topic,  but didn\u2019t know enough then to know what to ask. i think we have some more specific questions this time. We are planning a full kitchen renovation, and are trying to decide on how to handle the exhaust hood for a 36\u201d induction cooktop which will be located in an island. out goal is to have adequate ventilation for wok cooking, while minimizing noise, and and, of course, not spending more than is necessary to accomplish all that. We\u2019re planning on installing 42\u201d island hood, placed no more than 36 inches above the cooktop, possibly with some sort of decorative enclosure (We\u2019ve got a historic house, and think the industrial appearance of most hoods would be out of place.) Based on the direction of the joists, we expect to run the exhaust vent about 7 feet straight horIzontally to the exterior of the house. The kitchen volume is about 2100 cubic feet. I\u2019ve gotten mixed messages on just what CFMs I really need for this setup, maybe because induction usually requires lower CFM than gas, but wok cooking pushes the requirements back up. (Anything over 400 CFM will mean make up air, according to code.) The rule I\u2019ve seen in some places says that for electric cooktops, I can calculate the CFM I need by multiplying the cooktop width by 10, which gives me 360 CFM. If that is really sufficient, it could certainly save us some money. But I am skeptical that it will really do the trick, considering the style of cooking we do. Anyway, we went to a Wolf/Sub-Zero showroom to look at Best hoods in particular, because we\u2019d heard that they had particularly quiet blowers. The specialist there explained that with any run under 10 feet, putting the blower outside wouldn\u2019t help reduce noise enough to matter, even with a silencer, and that we were better off just getting a quieter internal blower.  Is this true? Taking all of this into consideration, we were looking at hoods from Best, specifically this one, which has an 800 CFM internal blower which is supposed to be unusually quiet, but the hood is labeled \u201dLimited quantities available\u201d,  making me think it might be discontinued. But I also understand that Best manufactured hoods for a lot of other brands (anyone know which ones?), so maybe I can find the same hood with some other \u201dlabel\u201d? Basically, my main question at this point is whether we seem to be on the right track. We want effective ventilation, we want it to be as quiet as is reasonably achievable. We are willing to pay what it takes to accomplish that, within reason. While we have a contractor for the overall project, we\u2019re not yet in touch with his HVAC person, who might be able to answer these questions, and we really have to get on with ordering appliances (including the hood), or we risk delaying the whole project.", "images": []}
